409010	[Illustration]
409026	
409028	Elizabeth, when Mr. Darcy gave her the letter, did not expect it to
409097	contain a renewal of his offers, she had formed no expectation at all of
409171	its contents. But such as they were, it may be well supposed how eagerly
409245	she went through them, and what a contrariety of emotion they excited.
409317	Her feelings as she read were scarcely to be defined. With amazement did
409391	she first understand that he believed any apology to be in his power;
409462	and steadfastly was she persuaded, that he could have no explanation to
409535	give, which a just sense of shame would not conceal. With a strong
409603	prejudice against everything he might say, she began his account of
409672	what had happened at Netherfield. She read with an eagerness which
409740	hardly left her power of comprehension; and from impatience of knowing
409812	what the next sentence might bring, was incapable of attending to the
409883	sense of the one before her eyes. His belief of her sister’s
409947	insensibility she instantly resolved to be false; and his account of the
410021	real, the worst objections to the match, made her too angry to have any
410094	wish of doing him justice. He expressed no regret for what he had done
410166	which satisfied her; his style was not penitent, but haughty. It was all
410240	pride and insolence.
410262	
410264	But when this subject was succeeded by his account of Mr. Wickham--when
410337	she read, with somewhat clearer attention, a relation of events which,
410409	if true, must overthrow every cherished opinion of his worth, and which
410482	bore so alarming an affinity to his own history of himself--her feelings
410556	were yet more acutely painful and more difficult of definition.
410621	Astonishment, apprehension, and even horror, oppressed her. She wished
410693	to discredit it entirely, repeatedly exclaiming, “This must be false!
410766	This cannot be! This must be the grossest falsehood!”--and when she had
410841	gone through the whole letter, though scarcely knowing anything of the
410913	last page or two, put it hastily away, protesting that she would not
410983	regard it, that she would never look in it again.
411034	
411036	In this perturbed state of mind, with thoughts that could rest on
411103	nothing, she walked on; but it would not do: in half a minute the letter
411177	was unfolded again; and collecting herself as well as she could, she
411247	again began the mortifying perusal of all that related to Wickham, and
411319	commanded herself so far as to examine the meaning of every sentence.
411390	The account of his connection with the Pemberley family was exactly
411459	what he had related himself; and the kindness of the late Mr. Darcy,
411529	though she had not before known its extent, agreed equally well with his
411603	own words. So far each recital confirmed the other; but when she came to
411677	the will, the difference was great. What Wickham had said of the living
411750	was fresh in her memory; and as she recalled his very words, it was
411819	impossible not to feel that there was gross duplicity on one side or the
411893	other, and, for a few moments, she flattered herself that her wishes did
411967	not err. But when she read and re-read, with the closest attention, the
412040	particulars immediately following of Wickham’s resigning all pretensions
412116	to the living, of his receiving in lieu so considerable a sum as three
412188	thousand pounds, again was she forced to hesitate. She put down the
412257	letter, weighed every circumstance with what she meant to be
412319	impartiality--deliberated on the probability of each statement--but with
412393	little success. On both sides it was only assertion. Again she read on.
412466	But every line proved more clearly that the affair, which she had
412533	believed it impossible that any contrivance could so represent as to
412603	render Mr. Darcy’s conduct in it less than infamous, was capable of a
412676	turn which must make him entirely blameless throughout the whole.
412743	
412745	The extravagance and general profligacy which he scrupled not to lay to
412818	Mr. Wickham’s charge exceedingly shocked her; the more so, as she could
412893	bring no proof of its injustice. She had never heard of him before his
412965	entrance into the ----shire militia, in which he had engaged at the
413034	persuasion of the young man, who, on meeting him accidentally in town,
413106	had there renewed a slight acquaintance. Of his former way of life,
413175	nothing had been known in Hertfordshire but what he told
413233

413336	himself. As to his real character, had information been in her power,

413476	manner, had established him at once in the possession of every virtue.
413548	She tried to recollect some instance of goodness, some distinguished
413618	trait of integrity or benevolence, that might rescue him from the
413685	attacks of Mr. Darcy; or at least, by the predominance of virtue, atone
413758	for those casual errors, under which she would endeavour to class what
413830	Mr. Darcy had described as the idleness and vice of many years’
413897	continuance. But no such recollection befriended her. She could see him
413970	instantly before her, in every charm of air and address, but she could
414042	remember no more substantial good than the general approbation of the
414113	neighbourhood, and the regard which his social powers had gained him in
414186	the mess. After pausing on this point a considerable while, she once
414256	more continued to read. But, alas! the story which followed, of his
414325	designs on Miss Darcy, received some confirmation from what had passed

414470	last she was referred for the truth of every particular to Colonel
414538	Fitzwilliam himself--from whom she had previously received the
414602	information of his near concern in all his cousin’s affairs and whose
414675	character she had no reason to question. At one time she had almost
414744	resolved on applying to him, but the idea was checked by the awkwardness
414818	of the application, and at length wholly banished by the conviction that
414892	Mr. Darcy would never have hazarded such a proposal, if he had not been
414965	well assured of his cousin’s corroboration.
415012

415083	between Wickham and herself in their first evening at Mr. Philips’s.
415155	Many of his expressions were still fresh in her memory. She was _now_
415226	struck with the impropriety of such communications to a stranger, and

416046

430085	see of the world, must make Hunsford extremely dull to a young lady like
430159	yourself; but I hope you will believe us grateful for the condescension,

466420	even the _appearance_ of what is right. His pride, in that direction,

466564	him from such foul misconduct as I have suffered by. I only fear that
466635	the sort of cautiousness to which you, I imagine, have been alluding, is

467641	between her and her family was rather noisy than pathetic. Kitty was the

467997	was every reason to believe would be attended to; and, in the clamorous
468070	happiness of Lydia herself in bidding farewell, the more gentle adieus

468260	CHAPTER XLII.
468275	
468277	
468279	[Illustration]
468295	
468297	Had Elizabeth’s opinion been all drawn from her own family, she could
468370	not have formed a very pleasing picture of conjugal felicity or domestic
468444	comfort. Her father, captivated by youth and beauty, and that appearance
468518	of good-humour which youth and beauty generally give, had married a
468587	woman whose weak understanding and illiberal mind had very early in
468656	their marriage put an end to all real affection for her. Respect,
468723	esteem, and confidence had vanished for ever; and all his views of
468791	domestic happiness were overthrown. But Mr. Bennet was not of a
468856	disposition to seek comfort for the disappointment which his own
468922	imprudence had brought on in any of those pleasures which too often
468991	console the unfortunate for their folly or their vice. He was fond of
469062	the country and of books; and from these tastes had arisen his principal
469136	enjoyments. To his wife he was very little otherwise indebted than as
469207	her ignorance and folly had contributed to his amusement. This is not
469278	the sort of happiness which a man would in general wish to owe to his
469349	wife; but where other powers of entertainment are wanting, the true
469418	philosopher will derive benefit from such as are given.
469475	
469477	Elizabeth, however, had never been blind to the impropriety of her
469545	father’s behaviour as a husband. She had always seen it with pain; but
469619	respecting his abilities, and grateful for his affectionate treatment of
469693	herself, she endeavoured to forget what she could not overlook, and to
469765	banish from her thoughts that continual breach of conjugal obligation
469836	and decorum which, in exposing his wife to the contempt of her own
469904	children, was so highly reprehensible. But she had never felt so
469970	strongly as now the disadvantages which must attend the children of so
470042	unsuitable a marriage, nor ever been so fully aware of the evils arising
470116	from so ill-judged a direction of talents--talents which, rightly used,
470189	might at least have preserved the respectability of his daughters, even
470262	if incapable of enlarging the mind of his wife.
470311	
470313	When Elizabeth had rejoiced over Wickham’s departure, she found little
470387	other cause for satisfaction in the loss of the regiment. Their parties
470460	abroad were less varied than before; and at home she had a mother and
470531	sister, whose constant repinings at the dulness of everything around
470601	them threw a real gloom over their domestic circle; and, though Kitty
470672	might in time regain her natural degree of sense, since the disturbers
470744	of her brain were removed, her other sister, from whose disposition
470813	greater evil might be apprehended, was likely to be hardened in all her
470886	folly and assurance, by a situation of such double danger as a
470950	watering-place and a camp. Upon the whole, therefore, she found, what
471021	has been sometimes found before, that an event to which she had looked
471093	forward with impatient desire, did not, in taking place, bring all the
471165	satisfaction she had promised herself. It was consequently necessary to
471238	name some other period for the commencement of actual felicity; to have
471311	some other point on which her wishes and hopes might be fixed, and by
471382	again enjoying the pleasure of anticipation, console herself for the
471452	present, and prepare for another disappointment. Her tour to the Lakes
471524	was now the object of her happiest thoughts: it was her best consolation
471598	for all the uncomfortable hours which the discontentedness of her mother
471672	and Kitty made inevitable; and could she have included Jane in the
471740	scheme, every part of it would have been perfect.
471791	
471793	“But it is fortunate,” thought she, “that I have something to wish for.
471872	Were the whole arrangement complete, my disappointment would be certain.
471946	But here, by carrying with me one ceaseless source of regret in my
472014	sister’s absence, I may reasonably hope to have all my expectations of
472088	pleasure realized. A scheme of which every part promises delight can
472158	never be successful; and general disappointment is only warded off by
472229	the defence of some little peculiar vexation.”
472279	
472281	When Lydia went away she promised to write very often and very minutely
472354	to her mother and Kitty; but her letters were always long expected, and
472427	always very short. Those to her mother contained little else than that
472499	they were just returned from the library, where such and such officers
472571	had attended them, and where she had seen such beautiful ornaments as
472642	made her quite wild; that she had a new gown, or a new parasol, which
472713	she would have described more fully, but was obliged to leave off in a
472785	violent hurry, as Mrs. Forster called her, and they were going to the
472856	camp; and from her correspondence with her sister there was still less
472928	to be learnt, for her letters to Kitty, though rather longer, were much
473001	too full of lines under the words to be made public.

473057	After the first fortnight or three weeks of her absence, health,
473123	good-humour, and cheerfulness began to reappear at Longbourn. Everything
473197	wore a happier aspect. The families who had been in town for the winter
473270	came back again, and summer finery and summer engagements arose. Mrs.
473341	Bennet was restored to her usual querulous serenity; and by the middle
473413	of June Kitty was so much recovered as to be able to enter Meryton
473481	without tears,--an event of such happy promise as to make Elizabeth
473550	hope, that by the following Christmas she might be so tolerably
473615	reasonable as not to mention an officer above once a day, unless, by
473685	some cruel and malicious arrangement at the War Office, another regiment
473759	should be quartered in Meryton.
473792

473864	approaching; and a fortnight only was wanting of it, when a letter
473932	arrived from Mrs. Gardiner, which at once delayed its commencement and
474004	curtailed its extent. Mr. Gardiner would be prevented by business from
474076	setting out till a fortnight later in July, and must be in London again

474220	far, and see so much as they had proposed, or at least to see it with

474722	they were now to spend a few days, was probably as great an object of
474793	her curiosity as all the celebrated beauties of Matlock, Chatsworth,
474863	Dovedale, or the Peak.
474887	
474889	Elizabeth was excessively disappointed: she had set her heart on seeing
474962	the Lakes; and still thought there might have been time enough. But it
475034	was her business to be satisfied--and certainly her temper to be happy;
475107	and all was soon right again.

475213	impossible for her to see the word without thinking of Pemberley and its
475287	owner. “But surely,” said she, “I may enter his county with impunity,

475583	Mrs. Gardiner, with their four children, did at length appear at
475649	Longbourn. The children, two girls of six and eight years old, and two
475721	younger boys, were to be left under the particular care of their cousin
475794	Jane, who was the general favourite, and whose steady sense and
475859	sweetness of temper exactly adapted her for attending to them in every
475931	way--teaching them, playing with them, and loving them.
475988	
475990	The Gardiners stayed only one night at Longbourn, and set off the next
476062	morning with Elizabeth in pursuit of novelty and amusement. One
476127	enjoyment was certain--that of suitableness as companions; a
476189	suitableness which comprehended health and temper to bear
476248	inconveniences--cheerfulness to enhance every pleasure--and affection
476319	and intelligence, which might supply it among themselves if there were
476391	disappointments abroad.

477042	was not in their direct road; nor more than a mile or two out of it. In

477392	much?” said her aunt. “A place, too, with which so many of your
477461	acquaintance are connected. Wickham passed all his youth there, you
477530	know.”
477540

479338	Pemberley Woods with some perturbation; and when at length they turned
479410	in at the lodge, her spirits were in a high flutter.

479536	entered it in one of its lowest points, and drove for some time through
479609	a beautiful wood stretching over a wide extent.

479735	every remarkable spot and point of view. They gradually ascended for

479874	eminence, where the wood ceased, and the eye was instantly caught by
479944	Pemberley House, situated on the opposite side of the valley, into which
480018	the road with some abruptness wound. It was a large, handsome stone
480087	building, standing well on rising ground, and backed by a ridge of high
480160	woody hills; and in front a stream of some natural importance was
480227	swelled into greater, but without any artificial appearance. Its banks
480299	were neither formal nor falsely adorned. Elizabeth was delighted. She

480443	beauty had been so little counteracted by an awkward taste. They were
480514	all of them warm in their admiration; and at that moment she felt that

480997	wonder at her being where she was.

481105	fine, and more civil, than she had any notion of finding her. They

517839	nothing to accuse him of but pride; pride he probably had, and if not,
517911	it would certainly be imputed by the inhabitants of a small market town
517984	where the family did not visit. It was acknowledged, however, that he
518055	was a liberal man, and did much good among the poor.
518109	
518111	With respect to Wickham, the travellers soon found that he was not held
518184	there in much estimation; for though the chief of his concerns with the
518257	son of his patron were imperfectly understood, it was yet a well-known
518329	fact that, on his quitting Derbyshire, he had left many debts behind
518399	him, which Mr. Darcy afterwards discharged.
518444

518519	the last; and the evening, though as it passed it seemed long, was not

520199	means unpleasing, though it could not be exactly defined. She respected,

521486	Convinced as Elizabeth now was that Miss Bingley’s dislike of her had
521559	originated in jealousy, she could not help feeling how very unwelcome
521630	her appearance at Pemberley must be to her, and was curious to know
521699	with how much civility on that lady’s side the acquaintance would now
521772	be renewed.
521785	
521787	On reaching the house, they were shown through the hall into the saloon,
521861	whose northern aspect rendered it delightful for summer. Its windows,
521932	opening to the ground, admitted a most refreshing view of the high woody
522006	hills behind the house, and of the beautiful oaks and Spanish chestnuts
522079	which were scattered over the intermediate lawn.
522129	
522131	In this room they were received by Miss Darcy, who was sitting there
522201	with Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley, and the lady with whom she lived in
522272	London. Georgiana’s reception of them was very civil, but attended with
522347	all that embarrassment which, though proceeding from shyness and the
522417	fear of doing wrong, would easily give to those who felt themselves
522486	inferior the belief of her being proud and reserved. Mrs. Gardiner and
522558	her niece, however, did her justice, and pitied her.
522612	
522614	By Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley they were noticed only by a courtesy; and
522688	on their being seated, a pause, awkward as such pauses must always be,
522760	succeeded for a few moments. It was first broken by Mrs. Annesley, a
522830	genteel, agreeable-looking woman, whose endeavour to introduce some kind
522904	of discourse proved her to be more truly well-bred than either of the
522975	others; and between her and Mrs. Gardiner, with occasional help from
523045	Elizabeth, the conversation was carried on. Miss Darcy looked as if she
523118	wished for courage enough to join in it; and sometimes did venture a
523188	short sentence, when there was least danger of its being heard.
523253	
523255	Elizabeth soon saw that she was herself closely watched by Miss Bingley,
523329	and that she could not speak a word, especially to Miss Darcy, without
523401	calling her attention. This observation would not have prevented her
523471	from trying to talk to the latter, had they not been seated at an
523538	inconvenient distance; but she was not sorry to be spared the necessity
523611	of saying much: her own thoughts were employing her. She expected every
523684	moment that some of the gentlemen would enter the room: she wished, she
523757	feared, that the master of the house might be amongst them; and whether
523830	she wished or feared it most, she could scarcely determine. After
523897	sitting in this manner a quarter of an hour, without hearing Miss
523964	Bingley’s voice, Elizabeth was roused by receiving from her a cold
524034	inquiry after the health of her family. She answered with equal
524099	indifference and brevity, and the other said no more.
524154	
524156	The next variation which their visit afforded was produced by the
524223	entrance of servants with cold meat, cake, and a variety of all the
524292	finest fruits in season; but this did not take place till after many a
524364	significant look and smile from Mrs. Annesley to Miss Darcy had been
524434	given, to remind her of her post. There was now employment for the whole
524508	party; for though they could not all talk, they could all eat; and the
524580	beautiful pyramids of grapes, nectarines, and peaches, soon collected
524651	them round the table.
524674	
524676	While thus engaged, Elizabeth had a fair opportunity of deciding whether
524750	she most feared or wished for the appearance of Mr. Darcy, by the
524817	feelings which prevailed on his entering the room; and then, though but
524890	a moment before she had believed her wishes to predominate, she began to
524964	regret that he came.
524986

525059	gentlemen from the house, was engaged by the river; and had left him

526328	They must be a great loss to _your_ family.”
526376

526455	instantly comprehended that he was uppermost in her thoughts; and the

527733	hereafter her own. He had certainly formed such a plan; and without

531898	Elizabeth had been a good deal disappointed in not finding a letter from
531972	Jane on their first arrival at Lambton; and this disappointment had been
532046	renewed on each of the mornings that had now been spent there; but on
532117	the third her repining was over, and her sister justified, by the
532184	receipt of two letters from her at once, on one of which was marked that
532258	it had been mis-sent elsewhere. Elizabeth was not surprised at it, as
532329	Jane had written the direction remarkably ill.
532377

532449	uncle and aunt, leaving her to enjoy them in quiet, set off by
532513	themselves. The one mis-sent must be first attended to; it had been
532582	written five days ago. The beginning contained an account of all their
532654	little parties and engagements, with such news as the country afforded;
532727	but the latter half, which was dated a day later, and written in evident
532801	agitation, gave more important intelligence. It was to this effect:--
532872

532946	most unexpected and serious nature; but I am afraid of alarming you--be
533019	assured that we are all well. What I have to say relates to poor Lydia.
533092	An express came at twelve last night, just as we were all gone to bed,
533164	from Colonel Forster, to inform us that she was gone off to Scotland
533234	with one of his officers; to own the truth, with Wickham! Imagine our
533305	surprise. To Kitty, however, it does not seem so wholly unexpected. I am
533379	very, very sorry. So imprudent a match on both sides! But I am willing
533451	to hope the best, and that his character has been misunderstood.
533517	Thoughtless and indiscreet I can easily believe him, but this step (and
533590	let us rejoice over it) marks nothing bad at heart. His choice is
533657	disinterested at least, for he must know my father can give her nothing.
533731	Our poor mother is sadly grieved. My father bears it better. How
533797	thankful am I, that we never let them know what has been said against
533868	him; we must forget it ourselves. They were off Saturday night about
533938	twelve, as is conjectured, but were not missed till yesterday morning at
534012	eight. The express was sent off directly. My dear Lizzy, they must have
534085	passed within ten miles of us. Colonel Forster gives us reason to expect
534159	him here soon. Lydia left a few lines for his wife, informing her of
534229	their intention. I must conclude, for I cannot be long from my poor
534298	mother. I am afraid you will not be able to make it out, but I hardly
534369	know what I have written.”

534472	what she felt, Elizabeth, on finishing this letter, instantly seized the

534759	wish this may be more intelligible, but though not confined for time, my
534833	head is so bewildered that I cannot answer for being coherent. Dearest
534905	Lizzy, I hardly know what I would write, but I have bad news for you,

535047	and our poor Lydia would be, we are now anxious to be assured it has

573441	the great consolation of his sister, who considered it as the only

599203	
599205	[Illustration]

599223	Mr. Bennet had very often wished, before this period of his life, that,
599296	instead of spending his whole income, he had laid by an annual sum, for
599369	the better provision of his children, and of his wife, if she survived
599441	him. He now wished it more than ever. Had he done his duty in that
599509	respect, Lydia need not have been indebted to her uncle for whatever of
599582	honour or credit could now be purchased for her. The satisfaction of
599652	prevailing on one of the most worthless young men in Great Britain to
599723	be her husband might then have rested in its proper place.
599783	
599785	He was seriously concerned that a cause of so little advantage to anyone
599859	should be forwarded at the sole expense of his brother-in-law; and he
599930	was determined, if possible, to find out the extent of his assistance,
600002	and to discharge the obligation as soon as he could.
600056	
600058	When first Mr. Bennet had married, economy was held to be perfectly
600127	useless; for, of course, they were to have a son. This son was to join
600199	in cutting off the entail, as soon as he should be of age, and the widow
600273	and younger children would by that means be provided for. Five daughters
600347	successively entered the world, but yet the son was to come; and Mrs.
600418	Bennet, for many years after Lydia’s birth, had been certain that he
600490	would. This event had at last been despaired of, but it was then too
600560	late to be saving. Mrs. Bennet had no turn for economy; and her
600625	husband’s love of independence had alone prevented their exceeding their
600701	income.
600710	
600712	Five thousand pounds was settled by marriage articles on Mrs. Bennet and
600786	the children. But in what proportions it should be divided amongst the
600858	latter depended on the will of the parents. This was one point, with
600928	regard to Lydia at least, which was now to be settled, and Mr. Bennet
600999	could have no hesitation in acceding to the proposal before him. In
601068	terms of grateful acknowledgment for the kindness of his brother, though
601142	expressed most concisely, he then delivered on paper his perfect
601208	approbation of all that was done, and his willingness to fulfil the
601277	engagements that had been made for him. He had never before supposed
601347	that, could Wickham be prevailed on to marry his daughter, it would be
601419	done with so little inconvenience to himself as by the present
601483	arrangement. He would scarcely be ten pounds a year the loser, by the
601554	hundred that was to be paid them; for, what with her board and pocket
601625	allowance, and the continual presents in money which passed to her
601693	through her mother’s hands, Lydia’s expenses had been very little within
601771	that sum.
601782	
601784	That it would be done with such trifling exertion on his side, too, was
601857	another very welcome surprise; for his chief wish at present was to have
601931	as little trouble in the business as possible. When the first transports
602005	of rage which had produced his activity in seeking her were over, he
602075	naturally returned to all his former indolence. His letter was soon
602144	despatched; for though dilatory in undertaking business, he was quick in
602218	its execution. He begged to know further particulars of what he was
602287	indebted to his brother; but was too angry with Lydia to send any
602354	message to her.
602371	
602373	The good news quickly spread through the house; and with proportionate
602445	speed through the neighbourhood. It was borne in the latter with decent
602518	philosophy. To be sure, it would have been more for the advantage of
602588	conversation, had Miss Lydia Bennet come upon the town; or, as the
602656	happiest alternative, been secluded from the world in some distant
602724	farm-house. But there was much to be talked of, in marrying her; and the
602798	good-natured wishes for her well-doing, which had proceeded before from
602871	all the spiteful old ladies in Meryton, lost but little of their spirit
602944	in this change of circumstances, because with such a husband her misery
603017	was considered certain.
603042	
603044	It was a fortnight since Mrs. Bennet had been down stairs, but on this
603116	happy day she again took her seat at the head of her table, and in
603184	spirits oppressively high. No sentiment of shame gave a damp to her
603253	triumph. The marriage of a daughter, which had been the first object of
603326	her wishes since Jane was sixteen, was now on the point of
603386	accomplishment, and her thoughts and her words ran wholly on those
603454	attendants of elegant nuptials, fine muslins, new carriages, and
603520	servants. She was busily searching through the neighbourhood for a
603588	proper situation for her daughter; and, without knowing or considering
603660	what their income might be, rejected many as deficient in size and
603728	importance.
603741

603822	great house at Stoke, if the drawing-room were larger; but Ashworth is
603894	too far off. I could not bear to have her ten miles from me; and as for
603967	Purvis Lodge, the attics are dreadful.”

604079	servants remained. But when they had withdrawn, he said to her, “Mrs.

604223	daughter, let us come to a right understanding. Into _one_ house in this
604297	neighbourhood they shall never have admittance. I will not encourage the
604371	imprudence of either, by receiving them at Longbourn.”

604642	daughter. He protested that she should receive from him no mark of
604710	affection whatever on the occasion. Mrs. Bennet could hardly comprehend
604783	it. That his anger could be carried to such a point of inconceivable
604853	resentment as to refuse his daughter a privilege, without which her
604922	marriage would scarcely seem valid, exceeded all that she could believe
604995	possible. She was more alive to the disgrace, which her want of new
605064	clothes must reflect on her daughter’s nuptials, than to any sense of

605207	took place.

607144	there must be a triumph.

607860	family.

607945	could not imagine. But how little of permanent happiness could belong to

608088	stronger than their virtue, she could easily conjecture.

608213	acknowledgments he briefly replied, with assurances of his eagerness to
608286	promote the welfare of any of his family; and concluded with entreaties
608359	that the subject might never be mentioned to him again. The principal
608430	purport of his letter was to inform them, that Mr. Wickham had resolved

608611	marriage was fixed on. And I think you will agree with me, in
608674	considering a removal from that corps as highly advisable, both on his
608746	account and my niece’s. It is Mr. Wickham’s intention to go into the
608820	Regulars; and, among his former friends, there are still some who are
608891	able and willing to assist him in the army. He has the promise of an
608961	ensigncy in General----’s regiment, now quartered in the north. It is
609034	an advantage to have it so far from this part of the kingdom. He
609100	promises fairly; and I hope among different people, where they may each
609173	have a character to preserve, they will both be more prudent. I have
609243	written to Colonel Forster, to inform him of our present arrangements,
609315	and to request that he will satisfy the various creditors of Mr. Wickham
609389	in and near Brighton with assurances of speedy payment, for which I have
609463	pledged myself. And will you give yourself the trouble of carrying

609676	hope at least he has not deceived us. Haggerston has our directions, and
609750	all will be completed in a week. They will then join his regiment,
609818	unless they are first invited to Longbourn; and I understand from Mrs.
609890	Gardiner that my niece is very desirous of seeing you all before she
609960	leaves the south. She is well, and begs to be dutifully remembered to
610031	you and her mother.--Yours, etc.

612132	Their sister’s wedding-day arrived; and Jane and Elizabeth felt for her
612207	probably more than she felt for herself. The carriage was sent to meet
612279	them at----, and they were to return in it by dinnertime. Their arrival
612352	was dreaded by the elder Miss Bennets--and Jane more especially, who
612422	gave Lydia the feelings which would have attended herself, had _she_
612492	been the culprit, and was wretched in the thought of what her sister
612562	must endure.

612649	them. Smiles decked the face of Mrs. Bennet, as the carriage drove up to
612723	the door; her husband looked impenetrably grave; her daughters, alarmed,
612797	anxious, uneasy.
612815

612892	she ran into the room. Her mother stepped forwards, embraced her, and
612963	welcomed her with rapture; gave her hand with an affectionate smile to
613035	Wickham, who followed his lady; and wished them both joy, with an
613102	alacrity which showed no doubt of their happiness.

613230	so cordial. His countenance rather gained in austerity; and he scarcely
613303	opened his lips. The easy assurance of the young couple, indeed, was
613373	enough to provoke him.
613397

613469	Lydia still; untamed, unabashed, wild, noisy, and fearless. She turned
613541	from sister to sister, demanding their congratulations; and when at
613610	length they all sat down, looked eagerly round the room, took notice of
613683	some little alteration in it, and observed, with a laugh, that it was a
613756	great while since she had been there.

613867	were always so pleasing, that, had his character and his marriage been
613939	exactly what they ought, his smiles and his easy address, while he
614007	claimed their relationship, would have delighted them all. Elizabeth
614077	had not before believed him quite equal to such assurance; but she sat
614149	down, resolving within herself to draw no limits in future to the
614216	impudence of an impudent man. _She_ blushed, and Jane blushed; but the
614288	cheeks of the two who caused their confusion suffered no variation of
614359	colour.

614442	of them talk fast enough; and Wickham, who happened to sit near

614581	with a good-humoured ease, which she felt very unable to equal in her
614652	replies. They seemed each of them to have the happiest memories in the

617536	behind you; and I dare say I shall get husbands for them before the

617625

617706	particularly like your way of getting husbands.”

617833	had received his commission before he left London, and he was to join
617904	his regiment at the end of a fortnight.
617945	
617947	No one but Mrs. Bennet regretted that their stay would be so short; and
618020	she made the most of the time by visiting about with her daughter, and

618164	all; to avoid a family circle was even more desirable to such as did
618234	think than such as did not.
618263	
618265	Wickham’s affection for Lydia was just what Elizabeth had expected to
618338	find it; not equal to Lydia’s for him. She had scarcely needed her
618408	present observation to be satisfied, from the reason of things, that
618478	their elopement had been brought on by the strength of her love rather
618550	than by his; and she would have wondered why, without violently caring

618692	that his flight was rendered necessary by distress of circumstances; and
618766	if that were the case, he was not the young man to resist an opportunity
618840	of having a companion.
618864	
618866	Lydia was exceedingly fond of him. He was her dear Wickham on every
618935	occasion; no one was to be put in competition with him. He did
618999	everything best in the world; and she was sure he would kill more birds
619072	on the first of September than anybody else in the country.

619207	elder sisters, she said to Elizabeth,--
619248

619326	not by, when I told mamma, and the others, all about it. Are not you
619396	curious to hear how it was managed?”
619436	
619438	“No, really,” replied Elizabeth; “I think there cannot be too little
619514	said on the subject.”
619539	
619541	“La! You are so strange! But I must tell you how it went off. We were
619614	married, you know, at St. Clement’s, because Wickham’s lodgings were in
619691	that parish. And it was settled that we should all be there by eleven
619762	o’clock. My uncle and aunt and I were to go together; and the others
619834	were to meet us at the church.
619866	
619868	“Well, Monday morning came, and I was in such a fuss! I was so afraid,
619942	you know, that something would happen to put it off, and then I should
620014	have gone quite distracted. And there was my aunt, all the time I was
620085	dressing, preaching and talking away just as if she was reading a
620152	sermon. However, I did not hear above one word in ten, for I was
620218	thinking, you may suppose, of my dear Wickham. I longed to know whether
620291	he would be married in his blue coat.
620330	
620332	“Well, and so we breakfasted at ten as usual: I thought it would never
620406	be over; for, by the bye, you are to understand that my uncle and aunt
620478	were horrid unpleasant all the time I was with them. If you’ll believe
620552	me, I did not once put my foot out of doors, though I was there a
620619	fortnight. Not one party, or scheme, or anything! To be sure, London was
620693	rather thin, but, however, the Little Theatre was open.
620750	
620752	“Well, and so, just as the carriage came to the door, my uncle was
620822	called away upon business to that horrid man Mr. Stone. And then, you
620893	know, when once they get together, there is no end of it. Well, I was so
620967	frightened I did not know what to do, for my uncle was to give me away;
621040	and if we were beyond the hour we could not be married all day. But,
621110	luckily, he came back again in ten minutes’ time, and then we all set
621183	out. However, I recollected afterwards, that if he _had_ been prevented
621256	going, the wedding need not be put off, for Mr. Darcy might have done as
621330	well.”
621340	
621342	“Mr. Darcy!” repeated Elizabeth, in utter amazement.
621400	
621402	“Oh, yes! he was to come there with Wickham, you know. But, gracious me!
621478	I quite forgot! I ought not to have said a word about it. I promised
621548	them so faithfully! What will Wickham say? It was to be such a secret!”
621623	
621625	“If it was to be a secret,” said Jane, “say not another word on the
621700	subject. You may depend upon my seeking no further.”
621756	
621758	“Oh, certainly,” said Elizabeth, though burning with curiosity; “we will
621838	ask you no questions.”
621864	
621866	“Thank you,” said Lydia; “for if you did, I should certainly tell you
621943	all, and then Wickham would be so angry.”

621990	On such encouragement to ask, Elizabeth was forced to put it out of her
622063	power, by running away.
622088	
622090	But to live in ignorance on such a point was impossible; or at least it
622163	was impossible not to try for information. Mr. Darcy had been at her
622233	sister’s wedding. It was exactly a scene, and exactly among people,

622723	Lydia had dropped, if it were compatible with the secrecy which had been

622808

623850	
623852	Elizabeth had the satisfaction of receiving an answer to her letter as
623924	soon as she possibly could. She was no sooner in possession of it, than
623997	hurrying into the little copse, where she was least likely to be
624063	interrupted, she sat down on one of the benches, and prepared to be
624132	happy; for the length of the letter convinced her that it did not
624199	contain a denial.
624218	
624220	     /* RIGHT “Gracechurch Street, _Sept. 6_. */
624272	
624274	“My dear Niece,
624293	
624295	     “I have just received your letter, and shall devote this whole
624366	     morning to answering it, as I foresee that a _little_ writing will
624439	     not comprise what I have to tell you. I must confess myself
624505	     surprised by your application; I did not expect it from _you_.
624574	     Don’t think me angry, however, for I only mean to let you know,
624646	     that I had not imagined such inquiries to be necessary on _your_
624717	     side. If you do not choose to understand me, forgive my
624779	     impertinence. Your uncle is as much surprised as I am; and nothing
624852	     but the belief of your being a party concerned would have allowed
624924	     him to act as he has done. But if you are really innocent and
624992	     ignorant, I must be more explicit. On the very day of my coming
625062	     home from Longbourn, your uncle had a most unexpected visitor. Mr.
625135	     Darcy called, and was shut up with him several hours. It was all
625206	     over before I arrived; so my curiosity was not so dreadfully racked
625280	     as _yours_ seems to have been. He came to tell Mr. Gardiner that he
625354	     had found out where your sister and Mr. Wickham were, and that he
625426	     had seen and talked with them both--Wickham repeatedly, Lydia once.
625500	     From what I can collect, he left Derbyshire only one day after
625569	     ourselves, and came to town with the resolution of hunting for
625638	     them. The motive professed was his conviction of its being owing to
625712	     himself that Wickham’s worthlessness had not been so well known as
625787	     to make it impossible for any young woman of character to love or
625859	     confide in him. He generously imputed the whole to his mistaken
625929	     pride, and confessed that he had before thought it beneath him to
626001	     lay his private actions open to the world. His character was to
626071	     speak for itself. He called it, therefore, his duty to step
626137	     forward, and endeavour to remedy an evil which had been brought on
626210	     by himself. If he _had another_ motive, I am sure it would never
626281	     disgrace him. He had been some days in town before he was able to
626353	     discover them; but he had something to direct his search, which was
626427	     more than _we_ had; and the consciousness of this was another
626495	     reason for his resolving to follow us. There is a lady, it seems, a
626569	     Mrs. Younge, who was some time ago governess to Miss Darcy, and was
626643	     dismissed from her charge on some cause of disapprobation, though
626715	     he did not say what. She then took a large house in Edward Street,
626788	     and has since maintained herself by letting lodgings. This Mrs.
626858	     Younge was, he knew, intimately acquainted with Wickham; and he
626928	     went to her for intelligence of him, as soon as he got to town. But
627002	     it was two or three days before he could get from her what he
627070	     wanted. She would not betray her trust, I suppose, without bribery
627143	     and corruption, for she really did know where her friend was to be
627216	     found. Wickham, indeed, had gone to her on their first arrival in
627288	     London; and had she been able to receive them into her house, they
627361	     would have taken up their abode with her. At length, however, our
627433	     kind friend procured the wished-for direction. They were in ----
627504	     Street. He saw Wickham, and afterwards insisted on seeing Lydia.
627575	     His first object with her, he acknowledged, had been to persuade
627646	     her to quit her present disgraceful situation, and return to her
627717	     friends as soon as they could be prevailed on to receive her,
627785	     offering his assistance as far as it would go. But he found Lydia
627857	     absolutely resolved on remaining where she was. She cared for none
627930	     of her friends; she wanted no help of his; she would not hear of
628001	     leaving Wickham. She was sure they should be married some time or
628073	     other, and it did not much signify when. Since such were her
628140	     feelings, it only remained, he thought, to secure and expedite a
628211	     marriage, which, in his very first conversation with Wickham, he
628282	     easily learnt had never been _his_ design. He confessed himself
628352	     obliged to leave the regiment on account of some debts of honour
628423	     which were very pressing; and scrupled not to lay all the ill

628566	     resign his commission immediately; and as to his future situation,
628639	     he could conjecture very little about it. He must go somewhere, but
628713	     he did not know where, and he knew he should have nothing to live

628853	     Though Mr. Bennet was not imagined to be very rich, he would have

629709	     be seen; and Mr. Darcy found, on further inquiry, that your father

629853	     not judge your father to be a person whom he could so properly

630067	     and till the next day it was only known that a gentleman had called

630214	     uncle at home, and, as I said before, they had a great deal of talk

630359	     was not all settled before Monday: as soon as it was, the express

630502	     fancy, Lizzy, that obstinacy is the real defect of his character,

630646	     but _this_ is the true one. Nothing was to be done that he did not
630719	     do himself; though I am sure (and I do not speak it to be thanked,
630792	     therefore say nothing about it) your uncle would most readily have
630865	     settled the whole. They battled it together for a long time, which
630938	     was more than either the gentleman or lady concerned in it
631003	     deserved. But at last your uncle was forced to yield, and instead
631075	     of being allowed to be of use to his niece, was forced to put up

634893	The contents of this letter threw Elizabeth into a flutter of spirits,
634965	in which it was difficult to determine whether pleasure or pain bore the
635039	greatest share. The vague and unsettled suspicions which uncertainty had
635113	produced, of what Mr. Darcy might have been doing to forward her
635179	sister’s match--which she had feared to encourage, as an exertion of
635251	goodness too great to be probable, and at the same time dreaded to be
635322	just, from the pain of obligation--were proved beyond their greatest
635392	extent to be true! He had followed them purposely to town, he had taken
635465	on himself all the trouble and mortification attendant on such a
635531	research; in which supplication had been necessary to a woman whom he
635602	must abominate and despise, and where he was reduced to meet, frequently
635676	meet, reason with, persuade, and finally bribe the man whom he always
635747	most wished to avoid, and whose very name it was punishment to him to
635818	pronounce. He had done all this for a girl whom he could neither regard
635891	nor esteem. Her heart did whisper that he had done it for her. But it
635962	was a hope shortly checked by other considerations; and she soon felt
636033	that even her vanity was insufficient, when required to depend on his
636104	affection for her, for a woman who had already refused him, as able to
636176	overcome a sentiment so natural as abhorrence against relationship with
636249	Wickham. Brother-in-law of Wickham! Every kind of pride must revolt from
636323	the connection. He had, to be sure, done much. She was ashamed to think
636396	how much. But he had given a reason for his interference, which asked no
636470	extraordinary stretch of belief. It was reasonable that he should feel
636542	he had been wrong; he had liberality, and he had the means of exercising
636616	it; and though she would not place herself as his principal inducement,
636689	she could perhaps believe, that remaining partiality for her might
636757	assist his endeavours in a cause where her peace of mind must be
636823	materially concerned. It was painful, exceedingly painful, to know that

637614	subsisted between Mr. Darcy and herself.

641734	Mr. Wickham was so perfectly satisfied with this conversation, that he
641806	never again distressed himself, or provoked his dear sister Elizabeth,
641878	by introducing the subject of it; and she was pleased to find that she
641950	had said enough to keep him quiet.

697930	Darcy. It was a rational scheme, to be sure! but from what the report of
698004	their engagement could originate, Elizabeth was at a loss to imagine;
698075	till she recollected that _his_ being the intimate friend of Bingley,
698146	and _her_ being the sister of Jane, was enough, at a time when the
698214	expectation of one wedding made everybody eager for another, to supply
698286	the idea. She had not herself forgotten to feel that the marriage of her
698360	sister must bring them more frequently together. And her neighbours at
698432	Lucas Lodge, therefore, (for through their communication with the
698499	Collinses, the report, she concluded, had reached Lady Catherine,) had
698571	only set _that_ down as almost certain and immediate which _she_ had
698641	looked forward to as possible at some future time.

698769	feeling some uneasiness as to the possible consequence of her persisting

738486	I should be so reasonable as to admit it! But I wonder how long you
738555	_would_ have gone on, if you had been left to yourself. I wonder when
738626	you _would_ have spoken if I had not asked you! My resolution of
738692	thanking you for your kindness to Lydia had certainly great effect. _Too
738766	much_, I am afraid; for what becomes of the moral, if our comfort
738833	springs from a breach of promise, for I ought not to have mentioned the
738906	subject? This will never do.”
738939	
738941	“You need not distress yourself. The moral will be perfectly fair. Lady
739016	Catherine’s unjustifiable endeavours to separate us were the means of
739089	removing all my doubts. I am not indebted for my present happiness to
739160	your eager desire of expressing your gratitude. I was not in a humour to
739234	wait for an opening of yours. My aunt’s intelligence had given me hope,
739309	and I was determined at once to know everything.”
739362	
739364	“Lady Catherine has been of infinite use, which ought to make her happy,
739440	for she loves to be of use. But tell me, what did you come down to
739508	Netherfield for? Was it merely to ride to Longbourn and be embarrassed?
739581	or had you intended any more serious consequences?”
739636	
739638	“My real purpose was to see _you_, and to judge, if I could, whether I
739712	might ever hope to make you love me. My avowed one, or what I avowed to
739785	myself, was to see whether your sister was still partial to Bingley, and
739859	if she were, to make the confession to him which I have since made.”
739931	
739933	“Shall you ever have courage to announce to Lady Catherine what is to
740006	befall her?”
740022	
740024	“I am more likely to want time than courage, Elizabeth. But it ought to
740099	be done; and if you will give me a sheet of paper it shall be done
740167	directly.”
740181	
740183	“And if I had not a letter to write myself, I might sit by you, and
740254	admire the evenness of your writing, as another young lady once did. But
740328	I have an aunt, too, who must not be longer neglected.”
740387	
740389	From an unwillingness to confess how much her intimacy with Mr. Darcy
740460	had been overrated, Elizabeth had never yet answered Mrs. Gardiner’s
740532	long letter; but now, having _that_ to communicate which she knew would
740605	be most welcome, she was almost ashamed to find that her uncle and aunt
740678	had already lost three days of happiness, and immediately wrote as
740746	follows:--
740758	
740760	“I would have thanked you before, my dear aunt, as I ought to have done,
740836	for your long, kind, satisfactory detail of particulars; but, to say the
740910	truth, I was too cross to write. You supposed more than really existed.
740983	But _now_ suppose as much as you choose; give a loose to your fancy,
741053	indulge your imagination in every possible flight which the subject will
741127	afford, and unless you believe me actually married, you cannot greatly
741199	err. You must write again very soon, and praise him a great deal more
741270	than you did in your last. I thank you again and again, for not going to
741344	the Lakes. How could I be so silly as to wish it! Your idea of the
741412	ponies is delightful. We will go round the park every day. I am the
741481	happiest creature in the world. Perhaps other people have said so
741548	before, but no one with such justice. I am happier even than Jane; she
741620	only smiles, I laugh. Mr. Darcy sends you all the love in the world that
741694	can be spared from me. You are all to come to Pemberley at Christmas.
741765	Yours,” etc.
741781	
741783	Mr. Darcy’s letter to Lady Catherine was in a different style, and still
741859	different from either was what Mr. Bennet sent to Mr. Collins, in return
741933	for his last.
741948	
741950	     /* “Dear Sir, */
741975	
741977	     “I must trouble you once more for congratulations. Elizabeth will
742051	     soon be the wife of Mr. Darcy. Console Lady Catherine as well as
742122	     you can. But, if I were you, I would stand by the nephew. He has
742193	     more to give.
742213	
742215	“Yours sincerely,” etc.
742244	
742246	Miss Bingley’s congratulations to her brother on his approaching
742314	marriage were all that was affectionate and insincere. She wrote even to
742388	Jane on the occasion, to express her delight, and repeat all her former
742461	professions of regard. Jane was not deceived, but she was affected; and
742534	though feeling no reliance on her, could not help writing her a much
742604	kinder answer than she knew was deserved.
742647	
742649	The joy which Miss Darcy expressed on receiving similar information was
742722	as sincere as her brother’s in sending it. Four sides of paper were
742793	insufficient to contain all her delight, and all her earnest desire of
742865	being loved by her sister.
742893	
742895	Before any answer could arrive from Mr. Collins, or any congratulations
742968	to Elizabeth from his wife, the Longbourn family heard that the
743033	Collinses were come themselves to Lucas Lodge. The reason of this
743100	sudden removal was soon evident. Lady Catherine had been rendered so
743170	exceedingly angry by the contents of her nephew’s letter, that
743236	Charlotte, really rejoicing in the match, was anxious to get away till
743308	the storm was blown over. At such a moment, the arrival of her friend
743379	was a sincere pleasure to Elizabeth, though in the course of their
743447	meetings she must sometimes think the pleasure dearly bought, when she
743519	saw Mr. Darcy exposed to all the parading and obsequious civility of her
743593	husband. He bore it, however, with admirable calmness. He could even
743663	listen to Sir William Lucas, when he complimented him on carrying away
743735	the brightest jewel of the country, and expressed his hopes of their all
743809	meeting frequently at St. James’s, with very decent composure. If he did
743885	shrug his shoulders, it was not till Sir William was out of sight.
743953	
743955	Mrs. Philips’s vulgarity was another, and, perhaps, a greater tax on his
744031	forbearance; and though Mrs. Philips, as well as her sister, stood in
744102	too much awe of him to speak with the familiarity which Bingley’s
744171	good-humour encouraged; yet, whenever she _did_ speak, she must be
744239	vulgar. Nor was her respect for him, though it made her more quiet, at
744311	all likely to make her more elegant. Elizabeth did all she could to
744380	shield him from the frequent notice of either, and was ever anxious to
744452	keep him to herself, and to those of her family with whom he might
744520	converse without mortification; and though the uncomfortable feelings
744591	arising from all this took from the season of courtship much of its
744660	pleasure, it added to the hope of the future; and she looked forward
744730	with delight to the time when they should be removed from society so
744800	little pleasing to either, to all the comfort and elegance of their
744869	family party at Pemberley.
744897	
744899	
744901	
744903	
744905	[Illustration]
744921	
744923	
744925	
744927	
744929	CHAPTER LXI.
744943	
744945	
744947	[Illustration]
744963	
744965	Happy for all her maternal feelings was the day on which Mrs. Bennet got
745039	rid of her two most deserving daughters. With what delighted pride she
745111	afterwards visited Mrs. Bingley, and talked of Mrs. Darcy, may be
745178	guessed. I wish I could say, for the sake of her family, that the
745245	accomplishment of her earnest desire in the establishment of so many of
745318	her children produced so happy an effect as to make her a sensible,
745387	amiable, well-informed woman for the rest of her life; though, perhaps,
745460	it was lucky for her husband, who might not have relished domestic
745528	felicity in so unusual a form, that she still was occasionally nervous
745600	and invariably silly.
745623	
745625	Mr. Bennet missed his second daughter exceedingly; his affection for her
745699	drew him oftener from home than anything else could do. He delighted in
745772	going to Pemberley, especially when he was least expected.
745832	
745834	Mr. Bingley and Jane remained at Netherfield only a twelvemonth. So near
745908	a vicinity to her mother and Meryton relations was not desirable even to
745982	_his_ easy temper, or _her_ affectionate heart. The darling wish of his
746055	sisters was then gratified: he bought an estate in a neighbouring county
746129	to Derbyshire; and Jane and Elizabeth, in addition to every other source
746203	of happiness, were within thirty miles of each other.
746258	
746260	Kitty, to her very material advantage, spent the chief of her time with
746333	her two elder sisters. In society so superior to what she had generally
746406	known, her improvement was great. She was not of so ungovernable a
746474	temper as Lydia; and, removed from the influence of Lydia’s example, she
746550	became, by proper attention and management, less irritable, less
746616	ignorant, and less insipid. From the further disadvantage of Lydia’s
746688	society she was of course carefully kept; and though Mrs. Wickham
746755	frequently invited her to come and stay with her, with the promise of
746826	balls and young men, her father would never consent to her going.
746893	
746895	Mary was the only daughter who remained at home; and she was necessarily
746969	drawn from the pursuit of accomplishments by Mrs. Bennet’s being quite
747043	unable to sit alone. Mary was obliged to mix more with the world, but
747114	she could still moralize over every morning visit; and as she was no
747184	longer mortified by comparisons between her sisters’ beauty and her own,
747260	it was suspected by her father that she submitted to the change without
747333	much reluctance.
747351	
747353	As for Wickham and Lydia, their characters suffered no revolution from
747425	the marriage of her sisters. He bore with philosophy the conviction that
747499	Elizabeth must now become acquainted with whatever of his ingratitude
747570	and falsehood had before been unknown to her; and, in spite of
747634	everything, was not wholly without hope that Darcy might yet be
747699	prevailed on to make his fortune. The congratulatory letter which
747766	Elizabeth received from Lydia on her marriage explained to her that, by
747839	his wife at least, if not by himself, such a hope was cherished. The
747909	letter was to this effect:--
747939	
747941	     /* “My dear Lizzy, */
747971	
747973	     “I wish you joy. If you love Mr. Darcy half so well as I do my dear
748049	     Wickham, you must be very happy. It is a great comfort to have you
748122	     so rich; and when you have nothing else to do, I hope you will
748191	     think of us. I am sure Wickham would like a place at court very
748261	     much; and I do not think we shall have quite money enough to live
748333	     upon without some help. Any place would do of about three or four
748405	     hundred a year; but, however, do not speak to Mr. Darcy about it,
748477	     if you had rather not.
748506	
748508	“Yours,” etc.
748527	
748529	As it happened that Elizabeth had much rather not, she endeavoured in
748600	her answer to put an end to every entreaty and expectation of the kind.
748673	Such relief, however, as it was in her power to afford, by the practice
748746	of what might be called economy in her own private expenses, she
748812	frequently sent them. It had always been evident to her that such an
748882	income as theirs, under the direction of two persons so extravagant in
748954	their wants, and heedless of the future, must be very insufficient to
749025	their support; and whenever they changed their quarters, either Jane or
749098	herself were sure of being applied to for some little assistance towards
749172	discharging their bills. Their manner of living, even when the
749236	restoration of peace dismissed them to a home, was unsettled in the
749305	extreme. They were always moving from place to place in quest of a
749373	cheap situation, and always spending more than they ought. His affection
749447	for her soon sunk into indifference: hers lasted a little longer; and,
749519	in spite of her youth and her manners, she retained all the claims to
749590	reputation which her marriage had given her. Though Darcy could never
749661	receive _him_ at Pemberley, yet, for Elizabeth’s sake, he assisted him
749735	further in his profession. Lydia was occasionally a visitor there, when
749808	her husband was gone to enjoy himself in London or Bath; and with the
749879	Bingleys they both of them frequently stayed so long, that even
749944	Bingley’s good-humour was overcome, and he proceeded so far as to _talk_
750020	of giving them a hint to be gone.
750055	
750057	Miss Bingley was very deeply mortified by Darcy’s marriage; but as she
750131	thought it advisable to retain the right of visiting at Pemberley, she
750203	dropped all her resentment; was fonder than ever of Georgiana, almost as
750277	attentive to Darcy as heretofore, and paid off every arrear of civility
750350	to Elizabeth.
750365	
750367	Pemberley was now Georgiana’s home; and the attachment of the sisters
750440	was exactly what Darcy had hoped to see. They were able to love each
750510	other, even as well as they intended. Georgiana had the highest opinion
750583	in the world of Elizabeth; though at first she often listened with an
750654	astonishment bordering on alarm at her lively, sportive manner of
750721	talking to her brother. He, who had always inspired in herself a respect
750795	which almost overcame her affection, she now saw the object of open
750864	pleasantry. Her mind received knowledge which had never before fallen in
750938	her way. By Elizabeth’s instructions she began to comprehend that a
751009	woman may take liberties with her husband, which a brother will not
751078	always allow in a sister more than ten years younger than himself.
751146	
751148	Lady Catherine was extremely indignant on the marriage of her nephew;
751219	and as she gave way to all the genuine frankness of her character, in
751290	her reply to the letter which announced its arrangement, she sent him
751361	language so very abusive, especially of Elizabeth, that for some time
751432	all intercourse was at an end. But at length, by Elizabeth’s persuasion,
751508	he was prevailed on to overlook the offence, and seek a reconciliation;
751581	and, after a little further resistance on the part of his aunt, her
751650	resentment gave way, either to her affection for him, or her curiosity
751722	to see how his wife conducted herself; and she condescended to wait on
751794	them at Pemberley, in spite of that pollution which its woods had
751861	received, not merely from the presence of such a mistress, but the
751929	visits of her uncle and aunt from the city.
751974	
751976	With the Gardiners they were always on the most intimate terms. Darcy,
752048	as well as Elizabeth, really loved them; and they were both ever
752114	sensible of the warmest gratitude towards the persons who, by bringing
752186	her into Derbyshire, had been the means of uniting them.
