1694	PREFACE.
1704	
1706	[Illustration]
1722	
1724	
1726	_Walt Whitman has somewhere a fine and just distinction between “loving
1801	by allowance” and “loving with personal love.” This distinction applies
1880	to books as well as to men and women; and in the case of the not very
1951	numerous authors who are the objects of the personal affection, it
2019	brings a curious consequence with it. There is much more difference as
2091	to their best work than in the case of those others who are loved “by
2164	allowance” by convention, and because it is felt to be the right and
2236	proper thing to love them. And in the sect--fairly large and yet
2302	unusually choice--of Austenians or Janites, there would probably be
2371	found partisans of the claim to primacy of almost every one of the
2439	novels. To some the delightful freshness and humour of_ Northanger
2507	Abbey, _its completeness, finish, and_ entrain, _obscure the undoubted
2579	critical facts that its scale is small, and its scheme, after all, that
2652	of burlesque or parody, a kind in which the first rank is reached with
2724	difficulty._ Persuasion, _relatively faint in tone, and not enthralling
2797	in interest, has devotees who exalt above all the others its exquisite
2869	delicacy and keeping. The catastrophe of_ Mansfield Park _is admittedly
2942	theatrical, the hero and heroine are insipid, and the author has almost
3015	wickedly destroyed all romantic interest by expressly admitting that
3085	Edmund only took Fanny because Mary shocked him, and that Fanny might
3156	very likely have taken Crawford if he had been a little more assiduous;
3229	yet the matchless rehearsal-scenes and the characters of Mrs. Norris and
3303	others have secured, I believe, a considerable party for it._ Sense and
3376	Sensibility _has perhaps the fewest out-and-out admirers; but it does
3447	not want them._
3464	
3466	_I suppose, however, that the majority of at least competent votes
3534	would, all things considered, be divided between_ Emma _and the present
3607	book; and perhaps the vulgar verdict (if indeed a fondness for Miss
3676	Austen be not of itself a patent of exemption from any possible charge
3748	of vulgarity) would go for_ Emma. _It is the larger, the more varied, the
3823	more popular; the author had by the time of its composition seen rather
3896	more of the world, and had improved her general, though not her most
3966	peculiar and characteristic dialogue; such figures as Miss Bates, as the
4040	Eltons, cannot but unite the suffrages of everybody. On the other hand,
4113	I, for my part, declare for_ Pride and Prejudice _unhesitatingly. It
4183	seems to me the most perfect, the most characteristic, the most
4248	eminently quintessential of its author’s works; and for this contention
4323	in such narrow space as is permitted to me, I propose here to show
4391	cause._
4400	
4402	_In the first place, the book (it may be barely necessary to remind the
4475	reader) was in its first shape written very early, somewhere about 1796,
4549	when Miss Austen was barely twenty-one; though it was revised and
4616	finished at Chawton some fifteen years later, and was not published till
4690	1813, only four years before her death. I do not know whether, in this
4762	combination of the fresh and vigorous projection of youth, and the
4830	critical revision of middle life, there may be traced the distinct
4898	superiority in point of construction, which, as it seems to me, it
4966	possesses over all the others. The plot, though not elaborate, is almost
5040	regular enough for Fielding; hardly a character, hardly an incident
5109	could be retrenched without loss to the story. The elopement of Lydia
5180	and Wickham is not, like that of Crawford and Mrs. Rushworth, a_ coup de
5254	théâtre; _it connects itself in the strictest way with the course of the
5330	story earlier, and brings about the denouement with complete propriety.
5403	All the minor passages--the loves of Jane and Bingley, the advent of Mr.
5477	Collins, the visit to Hunsford, the Derbyshire tour--fit in after the
5548	same unostentatious, but masterly fashion. There is no attempt at the
5619	hide-and-seek, in-and-out business, which in the transactions between
5690	Frank Churchill and Jane Fairfax contributes no doubt a good deal to the
5764	intrigue of_ Emma, _but contributes it in a fashion which I do not think
5838	the best feature of that otherwise admirable book. Although Miss Austen
5911	always liked something of the misunderstanding kind, which afforded her
5984	opportunities for the display of the peculiar and incomparable talent to
6058	be noticed presently, she has been satisfied here with the perfectly
6128	natural occasions provided by the false account of Darcy’s conduct given
6204	by Wickham, and by the awkwardness (arising with equal naturalness) from
6278	the gradual transformation of Elizabeth’s own feelings from positive
6350	aversion to actual love. I do not know whether the all-grasping hand of
6423	the playwright has ever been laid upon_ Pride and Prejudice; _and I dare
6497	say that, if it were, the situations would prove not startling or
6564	garish enough for the footlights, the character-scheme too subtle and
6635	delicate for pit and gallery. But if the attempt were made, it would
6705	certainly not be hampered by any of those loosenesses of construction,
6777	which, sometimes disguised by the conveniences of which the novelist can
6851	avail himself, appear at once on the stage._
6897	
6899	_I think, however, though the thought will doubtless seem heretical to
6971	more than one school of critics, that construction is not the highest
7042	merit, the choicest gift, of the novelist. It sets off his other gifts
7114	and graces most advantageously to the critical eye; and the want of it
7186	will sometimes mar those graces--appreciably, though not quite
7250	consciously--to eyes by no means ultra-critical. But a very badly-built
7323	novel which excelled in pathetic or humorous character, or which
7389	displayed consummate command of dialogue--perhaps the rarest of all
7458	faculties--would be an infinitely better thing than a faultless plot
7528	acted and told by puppets with pebbles in their mouths. And despite the
7601	ability which Miss Austen has shown in working out the story, I for one
7674	should put_ Pride and Prejudice _far lower if it did not contain what
7745	seem to me the very masterpieces of Miss Austen’s humour and of her
7816	faculty of character-creation--masterpieces who may indeed admit John
7887	Thorpe, the Eltons, Mrs. Norris, and one or two others to their company,
7961	but who, in one instance certainly, and perhaps in others, are still
8031	superior to them._
8051	
8053	_The characteristics of Miss Austen’s humour are so subtle and delicate
8128	that they are, perhaps, at all times easier to apprehend than to
8194	express, and at any particular time likely to be differently
8256	apprehended by different persons. To me this humour seems to possess a
8328	greater affinity, on the whole, to that of Addison than to any other of
8401	the numerous species of this great British genus. The differences of
8471	scheme, of time, of subject, of literary convention, are, of course,
8541	obvious enough; the difference of sex does not, perhaps, count for much,
8615	for there was a distinctly feminine element in “Mr. Spectator,” and in
8691	Jane Austen’s genius there was, though nothing mannish, much that was
8764	masculine. But the likeness of quality consists in a great number of
8834	common subdivisions of quality--demureness, extreme minuteness of touch,
8908	avoidance of loud tones and glaring effects. Also there is in both a
8978	certain not inhuman or unamiable cruelty. It is the custom with those
9049	who judge grossly to contrast the good nature of Addison with the
9116	savagery of Swift, the mildness of Miss Austen with the boisterousness
9188	of Fielding and Smollett, even with the ferocious practical jokes that
9260	her immediate predecessor, Miss Burney, allowed without very much
9327	protest. Yet, both in Mr. Addison and in Miss Austen there is, though a
9400	restrained and well-mannered, an insatiable and ruthless delight in
9469	roasting and cutting up a fool. A man in the early eighteenth century,
9541	of course, could push this taste further than a lady in the early
9608	nineteenth; and no doubt Miss Austen’s principles, as well as her heart,
9684	would have shrunk from such things as the letter from the unfortunate
9755	husband in the_ Spectator, _who describes, with all the gusto and all the
9830	innocence in the world, how his wife and his friend induce him to play
9902	at blind-man’s-buff. But another_ Spectator _letter--that of the damsel
9977	of fourteen who wishes to marry Mr. Shapely, and assures her selected
10048	Mentor that “he admires your_ Spectators _mightily”--might have been
10122	written by a rather more ladylike and intelligent Lydia Bennet in the
10193	days of Lydia’s great-grandmother; while, on the other hand, some (I
10265	think unreasonably) have found “cynicism” in touches of Miss Austen’s
10342	own, such as her satire of Mrs. Musgrove’s self-deceiving regrets over
10416	her son. But this word “cynical” is one of the most misused in the
10488	English language, especially when, by a glaring and gratuitous
10552	falsification of its original sense, it is applied, not to rough and
10622	snarling invective, but to gentle and oblique satire. If cynicism means
10695	the perception of “the other side,” the sense of “the accepted hells
10771	beneath,” the consciousness that motives are nearly always mixed, and
10844	that to seem is not identical with to be--if this be cynicism, then
10913	every man and woman who is not a fool, who does not care to live in a
10984	fool’s paradise, who has knowledge of nature and the world and life, is
11059	a cynic. And in that sense Miss Austen certainly was one. She may even
11131	have been one in the further sense that, like her own Mr. Bennet, she
11202	took an epicurean delight in dissecting, in displaying, in setting at
11273	work her fools and her mean persons. I think she did take this delight,
11346	and I do not think at all the worse of her for it as a woman, while she
11419	was immensely the better for it as an artist._
11467	
11469	_In respect of her art generally, Mr. Goldwin Smith has truly observed
11541	that “metaphor has been exhausted in depicting the perfection of it,
11613	combined with the narrowness of her field;” and he has justly added that
11689	we need not go beyond her own comparison to the art of a miniature
11757	painter. To make this latter observation quite exact we must not use the
11831	term miniature in its restricted sense, and must think rather of Memling
11905	at one end of the history of painting and Meissonier at the other, than
11978	of Cosway or any of his kind. And I am not so certain that I should
12047	myself use the word “narrow” in connection with her. If her world is a
12123	microcosm, the cosmic quality of it is at least as eminent as the
12190	littleness. She does not touch what she did not feel herself called to
12262	paint; I am not so sure that she could not have painted what she did not
12336	feel herself called to touch. It is at least remarkable that in two very
12410	short periods of writing--one of about three years, and another of not
12482	much more than five--she executed six capital works, and has not left a
12555	single failure. It is possible that the romantic paste in her
12618	composition was defective: we must always remember that hardly
12682	anybody born in her decade--that of the eighteenth-century
12742	seventies--independently exhibited the full romantic quality. Even Scott
12816	required hill and mountain and ballad, even Coleridge metaphysics and
12887	German to enable them to chip the classical shell. Miss Austen was an
12958	English girl, brought up in a country retirement, at the time when
13026	ladies went back into the house if there was a white frost which might
13098	pierce their kid shoes, when a sudden cold was the subject of the
13165	gravest fears, when their studies, their ways, their conduct were
13232	subject to all those fantastic limits and restrictions against which
13302	Mary Wollstonecraft protested with better general sense than particular
13375	taste or judgment. Miss Austen, too, drew back when the white frost
13444	touched her shoes; but I think she would have made a pretty good journey
13518	even in a black one._
13541	
13543	_For if her knowledge was not very extended, she knew two things which
13615	only genius knows. The one was humanity, and the other was art. On the
13687	first head she could not make a mistake; her men, though limited, are
13758	true, and her women are, in the old sense, “absolute.” As to art, if she
13836	has never tried idealism, her realism is real to a degree which makes
13907	the false realism of our own day look merely dead-alive. Take almost any
13981	Frenchman, except the late M. de Maupassant, and watch him laboriously
14053	piling up strokes in the hope of giving a complete impression. You get
14125	none; you are lucky if, discarding two-thirds of what he gives, you can
14198	shape a real impression out of the rest. But with Miss Austen the
14265	myriad, trivial, unforced strokes build up the picture like magic.
14333	Nothing is false; nothing is superfluous. When (to take the present book
14407	only) Mr. Collins changed his mind from Jane to Elizabeth “while Mrs.
14480	Bennet was stirring the fire” (and we know_ how _Mrs. Bennet would have
14555	stirred the fire), when Mr. Darcy “brought his coffee-cup back_
14622	himself,” _the touch in each case is like that of Swift--“taller by the
14699	breadth of my nail”--which impressed the half-reluctant Thackeray with
14773	just and outspoken admiration. Indeed, fantastic as it may seem, I
14841	should put Miss Austen as near to Swift in some ways, as I have put her
14914	to Addison in others._
14938	
14940	_This Swiftian quality appears in the present novel as it appears
15007	nowhere else in the character of the immortal, the ineffable Mr.
15073	Collins. Mr. Collins is really_ great; _far greater than anything Addison
15148	ever did, almost great enough for Fielding or for Swift himself. It has
15221	been said that no one ever was like him. But in the first place,_ he
15291	_was like him; he is there--alive, imperishable, more real than hundreds
15365	of prime ministers and archbishops, of “metals, semi-metals, and
15433	distinguished philosophers.” In the second place, it is rash, I think,
15507	to conclude that an actual Mr. Collins was impossible or non-existent at
15581	the end of the eighteenth century. It is very interesting that we
15648	possess, in this same gallery, what may be called a spoiled first
15715	draught, or an unsuccessful study of him, in John Dashwood. The
15780	formality, the under-breeding, the meanness, are there; but the portrait
15854	is only half alive, and is felt to be even a little unnatural. Mr.
15922	Collins is perfectly natural, and perfectly alive. In fact, for all the
15995	“miniature,” there is something gigantic in the way in which a certain
16071	side, and more than one, of humanity, and especially eighteenth-century
16144	humanity, its Philistinism, its well-meaning but hide-bound morality,
16215	its formal pettiness, its grovelling respect for rank, its materialism,
16288	its selfishness, receives exhibition. I will not admit that one speech
16360	or one action of this inestimable man is incapable of being reconciled
16432	with reality, and I should not wonder if many of these words and actions
16506	are historically true._
16531	
16533	_But the greatness of Mr. Collins could not have been so satisfactorily
16606	exhibited if his creatress had not adjusted so artfully to him the
16674	figures of Mr. Bennet and of Lady Catherine de Bourgh. The latter, like
16747	Mr. Collins himself, has been charged with exaggeration. There is,
16815	perhaps, a very faint shade of colour for the charge; but it seems to me
16889	very faint indeed. Even now I do not think that it would be impossible
16961	to find persons, especially female persons, not necessarily of noble
17031	birth, as overbearing, as self-centred, as neglectful of good manners,
17103	as Lady Catherine. A hundred years ago, an earl’s daughter, the Lady
17175	Powerful (if not exactly Bountiful) of an out-of-the-way country parish,
17249	rich, long out of marital authority, and so forth, had opportunities of
17322	developing these agreeable characteristics which seldom present
17387	themselves now. As for Mr. Bennet, Miss Austen, and Mr. Darcy, and even
17460	Miss Elizabeth herself, were, I am inclined to think, rather hard on him
17534	for the “impropriety” of his conduct. His wife was evidently, and must
17610	always have been, a quite irreclaimable fool; and unless he had shot her
17684	or himself there was no way out of it for a man of sense and spirit but
17757	the ironic. From no other point of view is he open to any reproach,
17826	except for an excusable and not unnatural helplessness at the crisis of
17899	the elopement, and his utterances are the most acutely delightful in the
17973	consciously humorous kind--in the kind that we laugh with, not at--that
18046	even Miss Austen has put into the mouth of any of her characters. It is
18119	difficult to know whether he is most agreeable when talking to his wife,
18193	or when putting Mr. Collins through his paces; but the general sense of
18266	the world has probably been right in preferring to the first rank his
18337	consolation to the former when she maunders over the entail, “My dear,
18411	do not give way to such gloomy thoughts. Let us hope for better things.
18484	Let us flatter ourselves that_ I _may be the survivor;” and his inquiry
18559	to his colossal cousin as to the compliments which Mr. Collins has just
18632	related as made by himself to Lady Catherine, “May I ask whether these
18706	pleasing attentions proceed from the impulse of the moment, or are the
18778	result of previous study?” These are the things which give Miss Austen’s
18856	readers the pleasant shocks, the delightful thrills, which are felt by
18928	the readers of Swift, of Fielding, and we may here add, of Thackeray, as
19002	they are felt by the readers of no other English author of fiction
19070	outside of these four._
19095	
19097	_The goodness of the minor characters in_ Pride and Prejudice _has been
19170	already alluded to, and it makes a detailed dwelling on their beauties
19242	difficult in any space, and impossible in this. Mrs. Bennet we have
19311	glanced at, and it is not easy to say whether she is more exquisitely
19382	amusing or more horribly true. Much the same may be said of Kitty and
19453	Lydia; but it is not every author, even of genius, who would have
19520	differentiated with such unerring skill the effects of folly and
19586	vulgarity of intellect and disposition working upon the common
19650	weaknesses of woman at such different ages. With Mary, Miss Austen has
19722	taken rather less pains, though she has been even more unkind to her;
19793	not merely in the text, but, as we learn from those interesting
19858	traditional appendices which Mr. Austen Leigh has given us, in dooming
19930	her privately to marry “one of Mr. Philips’s clerks.” The habits of
20005	first copying and then retailing moral sentiments, of playing and
20072	singing too long in public, are, no doubt, grievous and criminal; but
20143	perhaps poor Mary was rather the scapegoat of the sins of blue stockings
20217	in that Fordyce-belectured generation. It is at any rate difficult not
20289	to extend to her a share of the respect and affection (affection and
20359	respect of a peculiar kind; doubtless), with which one regards Mr.
20427	Collins, when she draws the moral of Lydia’s fall. I sometimes wish
20498	that the exigencies of the story had permitted Miss Austen to unite
20567	these personages, and thus at once achieve a notable mating and soothe
20639	poor Mrs. Bennet’s anguish over the entail._
20687	
20689	_The Bingleys and the Gardiners and the Lucases, Miss Darcy and Miss de
20762	Bourgh, Jane, Wickham, and the rest, must pass without special comment,
20835	further than the remark that Charlotte Lucas (her egregious papa, though
20909	delightful, is just a little on the thither side of the line between
20979	comedy and farce) is a wonderfully clever study in drab of one kind, and
21053	that Wickham (though something of Miss Austen’s hesitation of touch in
21127	dealing with young men appears) is a not much less notable sketch in
21197	drab of another. Only genius could have made Charlotte what she is, yet
21270	not disagreeable; Wickham what he is, without investing him either with
21343	a cheap Don Juanish attractiveness or a disgusting rascality. But the
21414	hero and the heroine are not tints to be dismissed._
21468	
21470	_Darcy has always seemed to me by far the best and most interesting of
21542	Miss Austen’s heroes; the only possible competitor being Henry Tilney,
21616	whose part is so slight and simple that it hardly enters into
21679	comparison. It has sometimes, I believe, been urged that his pride is
21750	unnatural at first in its expression and later in its yielding, while
21821	his falling in love at all is not extremely probable. Here again I
21889	cannot go with the objectors. Darcy’s own account of the way in which
21962	his pride had been pampered, is perfectly rational and sufficient; and
22034	nothing could be, psychologically speaking, a_ causa verior _for its
22104	sudden restoration to healthy conditions than the shock of Elizabeth’s
22178	scornful refusal acting on a nature_ ex hypothesi _generous. Nothing in
22251	even our author is finer and more delicately touched than the change of
22324	his demeanour at the sudden meeting in the grounds of Pemberley. Had he
22397	been a bad prig or a bad coxcomb, he might have been still smarting
22466	under his rejection, or suspicious that the girl had come
22525	husband-hunting. His being neither is exactly consistent with the
22592	probable feelings of a man spoilt in the common sense, but not really
22663	injured in disposition, and thoroughly in love. As for his being in
22732	love, Elizabeth has given as just an exposition of the causes of that
22803	phenomenon as Darcy has of the conditions of his unregenerate state,
22873	only she has of course not counted in what was due to her own personal
22945	charm._
22954	
22956	_The secret of that charm many men and not a few women, from Miss Austen
23030	herself downwards, have felt, and like most charms it is a thing rather
23103	to be felt than to be explained. Elizabeth of course belongs to the_
23173	allegro _or_ allegra _division of the army of Venus. Miss Austen was
23243	always provokingly chary of description in regard to her beauties; and
23315	except the fine eyes, and a hint or two that she had at any rate
23381	sometimes a bright complexion, and was not very tall, we hear nothing
23452	about her looks. But her chief difference from other heroines of the
23522	lively type seems to lie first in her being distinctly clever--almost
23593	strong-minded, in the better sense of that objectionable word--and
23661	secondly in her being entirely destitute of ill-nature for all her
23729	propensity to tease and the sharpness of her tongue. Elizabeth can give
23802	at least as good as she gets when she is attacked; but she never
23868	“scratches,” and she never attacks first. Some of the merest
23934	obsoletenesses of phrase and manner give one or two of her early
24000	speeches a slight pertness, but that is nothing, and when she comes to
24072	serious business, as in the great proposal scene with Darcy (which is,
24144	as it should be, the climax of the interest of the book), and in the
24214	final ladies’ battle with Lady Catherine, she is unexceptionable. Then
24288	too she is a perfectly natural girl. She does not disguise from herself
24361	or anybody that she resents Darcy’s first ill-mannered personality with
24436	as personal a feeling. (By the way, the reproach that the ill-manners of
24510	this speech are overdone is certainly unjust; for things of the same
24580	kind, expressed no doubt less stiltedly but more coarsely, might have
24651	been heard in more than one ball-room during this very year from persons
24725	who ought to have been no worse bred than Darcy.) And she lets the
24793	injury done to Jane and the contempt shown to the rest of her family
24863	aggravate this resentment in the healthiest way in the world._
24927	
24929	_Still, all this does not explain her charm, which, taking beauty as a
25001	common form of all heroines, may perhaps consist in the addition to her
25074	playfulness, her wit, her affectionate and natural disposition, of a
25144	certain fearlessness very uncommon in heroines of her type and age.
25213	Nearly all of them would have been in speechless awe of the magnificent
25286	Darcy; nearly all of them would have palpitated and fluttered at the
25356	idea of proposals, even naughty ones, from the fascinating Wickham.
25425	Elizabeth, with nothing offensive, nothing_ viraginous, _nothing of the
25498	“New Woman” about her, has by nature what the best modern (not “new”)
25577	women have by education and experience, a perfect freedom from the idea
25650	that all men may bully her if they choose, and that most will away with
25723	her if they can. Though not in the least “impudent and mannish grown,”
25799	she has no mere sensibility, no nasty niceness about her. The form of
25870	passion common and likely to seem natural in Miss Austen’s day was so
25943	invariably connected with the display of one or the other, or both of
26014	these qualities, that she has not made Elizabeth outwardly passionate.
26086	But I, at least, have not the slightest doubt that she would have
26153	married Darcy just as willingly without Pemberley as with it, and
26220	anybody who can read between lines will not find the lovers’
26284	conversations in the final chapters so frigid as they might have looked
26357	to the Della Cruscans of their own day, and perhaps do look to the Della
26431	Cruscans of this._
26451	
26453	_And, after all, what is the good of seeking for the reason of
26517	charm?--it is there. There were better sense in the sad mechanic
26583	exercise of determining the reason of its absence where it is not. In
26654	the novels of the last hundred years there are vast numbers of young
26724	ladies with whom it might be a pleasure to fall in love; there are at
26795	least five with whom, as it seems to me, no man of taste and spirit can
26868	help doing so. Their names are, in chronological order, Elizabeth
26935	Bennet, Diana Vernon, Argemone Lavington, Beatrix Esmond, and Barbara
27006	Grant. I should have been most in love with Beatrix and Argemone; I
27075	should, I think, for mere occasional companionship, have preferred Diana
27149	and Barbara. But to live with and to marry, I do not know that any one
27221	of the four can come into competition with Elizabeth._
27277	
27279	_GEORGE SAINTSBURY._

35436	
35438	
35440	It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession
35513	of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.
35559	
35561	However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his
35633	first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds
35707	of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful
35775	property of some one or other of their daughters.
35826	
35828	“My dear Mr. Bennet,” said his lady to him one day, “have you heard that
35908	Netherfield Park is let at last?”
35945	
35947	Mr. Bennet replied that he had not.
35984	
35986	“But it is,” returned she; “for Mrs. Long has just been here, and she
36063	told me all about it.”
36089	
36091	Mr. Bennet made no answer.
36119	
36121	“Do not you want to know who has taken it?” cried his wife, impatiently.
36199	
36201	“_You_ want to tell me, and I have no objection to hearing it.”
36270	
36272	[Illustration:
36288	
36290	“He came down to see the place”
36327	
36329	[_Copyright 1894 by George Allen._]]
36367	
36369	This was invitation enough.
36398	
36400	“Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs. Long says that Netherfield is taken
36474	by a young man of large fortune from the north of England; that he came
36547	down on Monday in a chaise and four to see the place, and was so much
36618	delighted with it that he agreed with Mr. Morris immediately; that he is
36692	to take possession before Michaelmas, and some of his servants are to be
36766	in the house by the end of next week.”
36808	
36810	“What is his name?”
36835	
36837	“Bingley.”
36853	
36855	“Is he married or single?”
36887	
36889	“Oh, single, my dear, to be sure! A single man of large fortune; four or
36965	five thousand a year. What a fine thing for our girls!”
37024	
37026	“How so? how can it affect them?”
37065	
37067	“My dear Mr. Bennet,” replied his wife, “how can you be so tiresome? You
37147	must know that I am thinking of his marrying one of them.”
37209	
37211	“Is that his design in settling here?”
37255	
37257	“Design? Nonsense, how can you talk so! But it is very likely that he
37330	_may_ fall in love with one of them, and therefore you must visit him as
37404	soon as he comes.”
37426	
37428	“I see no occasion for that. You and the girls may go--or you may send
37502	them by themselves, which perhaps will be still better; for as you are
37574	as handsome as any of them, Mr. Bingley might like you the best of the
37646	party.”
37657	
37659	“My dear, you flatter me. I certainly _have_ had my share of beauty, but
37735	I do not pretend to be anything extraordinary now. When a woman has five
37809	grown-up daughters, she ought to give over thinking of her own beauty.”
37884	
37886	“In such cases, a woman has not often much beauty to think of.”
37955	
37957	“But, my dear, you must indeed go and see Mr. Bingley when he comes into
38033	the neighbourhood.”
38056	
38058	“It is more than I engage for, I assure you.”
38109	
38111	“But consider your daughters. Only think what an establishment it would
38186	be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go,
38256	merely on that account; for in general, you know, they visit no new
38325	comers. Indeed you must go, for it will be impossible for _us_ to visit
38398	him, if you do not.”
38422	
38424	“You are over scrupulous, surely. I dare say Mr. Bingley will be very
38497	glad to see you; and I will send a few lines by you to assure him of my
38570	hearty consent to his marrying whichever he chooses of the girls--though
38644	I must throw in a good word for my little Lizzy.”
38697	
38699	“I desire you will do no such thing. Lizzy is not a bit better than the
38774	others: and I am sure she is not half so handsome as Jane, nor half so
38846	good-humoured as Lydia. But you are always giving _her_ the preference.”
38922	
38924	“They have none of them much to recommend them,” replied he: “they are
39002	all silly and ignorant like other girls; but Lizzy has something more of
39076	quickness than her sisters.”
39108	
39110	“Mr. Bennet, how can you abuse your own children in such a way? You take
39186	delight in vexing me. You have no compassion on my poor nerves.”
39254	
39256	“You mistake me, my dear. I have a high respect for your nerves. They
39329	are my old friends. I have heard you mention them with consideration
39399	these twenty years at least.”
39432	
39434	“Ah, you do not know what I suffer.”
39476	
39478	“But I hope you will get over it, and live to see many young men of four
39554	thousand a year come into the neighbourhood.”
39603	
39605	“It will be no use to us, if twenty such should come, since you will not
39681	visit them.”
39697	
39699	“Depend upon it, my dear, that when there are twenty, I will visit them
39774	all.”
39783	
39785	Mr. Bennet was so odd a mixture of quick parts, sarcastic humour,
39852	reserve, and caprice, that the experience of three-and-twenty years had
39925	been insufficient to make his wife understand his character. _Her_ mind
39998	was less difficult to develope. She was a woman of mean understanding,
40070	little information, and uncertain temper. When she was discontented, she
40144	fancied herself nervous. The business of her life was to get her
40210	daughters married: its solace was visiting and news.

40492	
40494	Mr. Bennet was among the earliest of those who waited on Mr. Bingley. He
40568	had always intended to visit him, though to the last always assuring his
40642	wife that he should not go; and till the evening after the visit was
40712	paid she had no knowledge of it. It was then disclosed in the following
40785	manner. Observing his second daughter employed in trimming a hat, he
40855	suddenly addressed her with,--
40887	
40889	“I hope Mr. Bingley will like it, Lizzy.”
40936	
40938	“We are not in a way to know _what_ Mr. Bingley likes,” said her mother,
41016	resentfully, “since we are not to visit.”
41063	
41065	“But you forget, mamma,” said Elizabeth, “that we shall meet him at the
41144	assemblies, and that Mrs. Long has promised to introduce him.”
41210	
41212	“I do not believe Mrs. Long will do any such thing. She has two nieces
41286	of her own. She is a selfish, hypocritical woman, and I have no opinion
41359	of her.”
41371	
41373	“No more have I,” said Mr. Bennet; “and I am glad to find that you do
41450	not depend on her serving you.”
41485	
41487	Mrs. Bennet deigned not to make any reply; but, unable to contain
41554	herself, began scolding one of her daughters.
41601	
41603	“Don’t keep coughing so, Kitty, for heaven’s sake! Have a little
41675	compassion on my nerves. You tear them to pieces.”
41729	
41731	“Kitty has no discretion in her coughs,” said her father; “she times
41807	them ill.”
41821	
41823	“I do not cough for my own amusement,” replied Kitty, fretfully. “When
41901	is your next ball to be, Lizzy?”
41937	
41939	“To-morrow fortnight.”
41967	
41969	“Ay, so it is,” cried her mother, “and Mrs. Long does not come back till
42049	the day before; so, it will be impossible for her to introduce him, for
42122	she will not know him herself.”
42157	
42159	“Then, my dear, you may have the advantage of your friend, and introduce
42235	Mr. Bingley to _her_.”
42261	
42263	“Impossible, Mr. Bennet, impossible, when I am not acquainted with him
42337	myself; how can you be so teasing?”
42376	
42378	“I honour your circumspection. A fortnight’s acquaintance is certainly
42454	very little. One cannot know what a man really is by the end of a
42521	fortnight. But if _we_ do not venture, somebody else will; and after
42591	all, Mrs. Long and her nieces must stand their chance; and, therefore,
42663	as she will think it an act of kindness, if you decline the office, I
42734	will take it on myself.”
42762	
42764	The girls stared at their father. Mrs. Bennet said only, “Nonsense,
42835	nonsense!”
42849	
42851	“What can be the meaning of that emphatic exclamation?” cried he. “Do
42928	you consider the forms of introduction, and the stress that is laid on
43000	them, as nonsense? I cannot quite agree with you _there_. What say you,
43073	Mary? For you are a young lady of deep reflection, I know, and read
43142	great books, and make extracts.”
43178	
43180	Mary wished to say something very sensible, but knew not how.
43243	
43245	“While Mary is adjusting her ideas,” he continued, “let us return to Mr.
43325	Bingley.”
43338	
43340	“I am sick of Mr. Bingley,” cried his wife.
43389	
43391	“I am sorry to hear _that_; but why did you not tell me so before? If I
43466	had known as much this morning, I certainly would not have called on
43536	him. It is very unlucky; but as I have actually paid the visit, we
43604	cannot escape the acquaintance now.”
43644	
43646	The astonishment of the ladies was just what he wished--that of Mrs.
43716	Bennet perhaps surpassing the rest; though when the first tumult of joy
43789	was over, she began to declare that it was what she had expected all the
43863	while.
43871	
43873	“How good it was in you, my dear Mr. Bennet! But I knew I should
43941	persuade you at last. I was sure you loved your girls too well to
44008	neglect such an acquaintance. Well, how pleased I am! And it is such a
44080	good joke, too, that you should have gone this morning, and never said a
44154	word about it till now.”
44182	
44184	“Now, Kitty, you may cough as much as you choose,” said Mr. Bennet; and,
44262	as he spoke, he left the room, fatigued with the raptures of his wife.
44334

44413	shut. “I do not know how you will ever make him amends for his kindness;

44555	pleasant, I can tell you, to be making new acquaintances every day; but
44628	for your sakes we would do anything. Lydia, my love, though you _are_

45190	
45192	Not all that Mrs. Bennet, however, with the assistance of her five
45260	daughters, could ask on the subject, was sufficient to draw from her
45330	husband any satisfactory description of Mr. Bingley. They attacked him
45402	in various ways, with barefaced questions, ingenious suppositions, and
45474	distant surmises; but he eluded the skill of them all; and they were at
45547	last obliged to accept the second-hand intelligence of their neighbour,
45620	Lady Lucas. Her report was highly favourable. Sir William had been
45688	delighted with him. He was quite young, wonderfully handsome, extremely
45761	agreeable, and, to crown the whole, he meant to be at the next assembly
45834	with a large party. Nothing could be more delightful! To be fond of
45903	dancing was a certain step towards falling in love; and very lively
45972	hopes of Mr. Bingley’s heart were entertained.
46022	
46024	“If I can but see one of my daughters happily settled at Netherfield,”
46100	said Mrs. Bennet to her husband, “and all the others equally well
46169	married, I shall have nothing to wish for.”
46216	
46218	In a few days Mr. Bingley returned Mr. Bennet’s visit, and sat about ten
46294	minutes with him in his library. He had entertained hopes of being
46362	admitted to a sight of the young ladies, of whose beauty he had heard
46433	much; but he saw only the father. The ladies were somewhat more
46498	fortunate, for they had the advantage of ascertaining, from an upper
46568	window, that he wore a blue coat and rode a black horse.
46626	
46628	An invitation to dinner was soon afterwards despatched; and already had
46701	Mrs. Bennet planned the courses that were to do credit to her
46764	housekeeping, when an answer arrived which deferred it all. Mr. Bingley
46837	was obliged to be in town the following day, and consequently unable to
46910	accept the honour of their invitation, etc. Mrs. Bennet was quite
46977	disconcerted. She could not imagine what business he could have in town
47050	so soon after his arrival in Hertfordshire; and she began to fear that
47122	he might always be flying about from one place to another, and never
47192	settled at Netherfield as he ought to be. Lady Lucas quieted her fears a
47266	little by starting the idea of his
47302	
47304	[Illustration:
47320	
47322	     “When the Party entered”
47357	
47359	[_Copyright 1894 by George Allen._]]
47397	
47399	being gone to London only to get a large party for the ball; and a
47467	report soon followed that Mr. Bingley was to bring twelve ladies and
47537	seven gentlemen with him to the assembly. The girls grieved over such a
47610	number of ladies; but were comforted the day before the ball by hearing
47683	that, instead of twelve, he had brought only six with him from London,
47755	his five sisters and a cousin. And when the party entered the
47818	assembly-room, it consisted of only five altogether: Mr. Bingley, his
47889	two sisters, the husband of the eldest, and another young man.
47953	
47955	Mr. Bingley was good-looking and gentlemanlike: he had a pleasant
48022	countenance, and easy, unaffected manners. His sisters were fine women,
48095	with an air of decided fashion. His brother-in-law, Mr. Hurst, merely
48166	looked the gentleman; but his friend Mr. Darcy soon drew the attention
48238	of the room by his fine, tall person, handsome features, noble mien, and
48312	the report, which was in general circulation within five minutes after
48384	his entrance, of his having ten thousand a year. The gentlemen
48448	pronounced him to be a fine figure of a man, the ladies declared he was
48521	much handsomer than Mr. Bingley, and he was looked at with great
48587	admiration for about half the evening, till his manners gave a disgust
48659	which turned the tide of his popularity; for he was discovered to be
48729	proud, to be above his company, and above being pleased; and not all his
48803	large estate in Derbyshire could save him from having a most forbidding,
48877	disagreeable countenance, and being unworthy to be compared with his
48947	friend.
48956	
48958	Mr. Bingley had soon made himself acquainted with all the principal
49027	people in the room: he was lively and unreserved, danced every dance,
49098	was angry that the ball closed so early, and talked of giving one
49165	himself at Netherfield. Such amiable qualities must speak for
49228	themselves. What a contrast between him and his friend! Mr. Darcy danced
49302	only once with Mrs. Hurst and once with Miss Bingley, declined being
49372	introduced to any other lady, and spent the rest of the evening in
49440	walking about the room, speaking occasionally to one of his own party.
49512	His character was decided. He was the proudest, most disagreeable man in
49586	the world, and everybody hoped that he would never come there again.
49656	Amongst the most violent against him was Mrs. Bennet, whose dislike of
49728	his general behaviour was sharpened into particular resentment by his
49799	having slighted one of her daughters.
49838	
49840	Elizabeth Bennet had been obliged, by the scarcity of gentlemen, to sit
49913	down for two dances; and during part of that time, Mr. Darcy had been
49984	standing near enough for her to overhear a conversation between him and
50057	Mr. Bingley, who came from the dance for a few minutes to press his
50126	friend to join it.
50146	
50148	“Come, Darcy,” said he, “I must have you dance. I hate to see you
50221	standing about by yourself in this stupid manner. You had much better
50292	dance.”
50303	
50305	“I certainly shall not. You know how I detest it, unless I am
50370	particularly acquainted with my partner. At such an assembly as this, it
50444	would be insupportable. Your sisters are engaged, and there is not
50512	another woman in the room whom it would not be a punishment to me to
50582	stand up with.”
50601	
50603	“I would not be so fastidious as you are,” cried Bingley, “for a
50675	kingdom! Upon my honour, I never met with so many pleasant girls in my
50747	life as I have this evening; and there are several of them, you see,
50817	uncommonly pretty.”
50840	
50842	“_You_ are dancing with the only handsome girl in the room,” said Mr.
50917	Darcy, looking at the eldest Miss Bennet.
50960	
50962	“Oh, she is the most beautiful creature I ever beheld! But there is one
51037	of her sisters sitting down just behind you, who is very pretty, and I
51109	dare say very agreeable. Do let me ask my partner to introduce you.”

51412	“She is tolerable: but not handsome enough to tempt _me_; and I am in no
51488	humour at present to give consequence to young ladies who are slighted

51680	Mr. Bingley followed his advice. Mr. Darcy walked off; and Elizabeth
51750	remained with no very cordial feelings towards him. She told the story,

51892	playful disposition, which delighted in anything ridiculous.

51956	The evening altogether passed off pleasantly to the whole family. Mrs.
52028	Bennet had seen her eldest daughter much admired by the Netherfield
52097	party. Mr. Bingley had danced with her twice, and she had been
52161	distinguished by his sisters. Jane was as much gratified by this as her
52234	mother could be, though in a quieter way. Elizabeth felt Jane’s
52301	pleasure. Mary had heard herself mentioned to Miss Bingley as the most
52373	accomplished girl in the neighbourhood; and Catherine and Lydia had been
52447	fortunate enough to be never without partners, which was all that they
52519	had yet learnt to care for at a ball. They returned, therefore, in good
52592	spirits to Longbourn, the village where they lived, and of which they
52663	were the principal inhabitants. They found Mr. Bennet still up. With a
52735	book, he was regardless of time; and on the present occasion he had a
52806	good deal of curiosity as to the event of an evening which had raised
52877	such splendid expectations. He had rather hoped that all his wife’s
52948	views on the stranger would be disappointed; but he soon found that he
53020	had a very different story to hear.
53057	
53059	“Oh, my dear Mr. Bennet,” as she entered the room, “we have had a most
53137	delightful evening, a most excellent ball. I wish you had been there.
53208	Jane was so admired, nothing could be like it. Everybody said how well
53280	she looked; and Mr. Bingley thought her quite beautiful, and danced with
53354	her twice. Only think of _that_, my dear: he actually danced with her
53425	twice; and she was the only creature in the room that he asked a second
53498	time. First of all, he asked Miss Lucas. I was so vexed to see him stand

53645	can, you know; and he seemed quite struck with Jane as she was going

55234

55254	
55256	When Jane and Elizabeth were alone, the former, who had been cautious in
55330	her praise of Mr. Bingley before, expressed to her sister how very much
55403	she admired him.
55421	
55423	“He is just what a young-man ought to be,” said she, “sensible,
55494	good-humoured, lively; and I never saw such happy manners! so much ease,
55568	with such perfect good breeding!”
55605

55681	likewise to be if he possibly can. His character is thereby complete.”
55755

55830	did not expect such a compliment.”
55868	
55870	“Did not you? _I_ did for you. But that is one great difference between
55945	us. Compliments always take _you_ by surprise, and _me_ never. What
56014	could be more natural than his asking you again? He could not help
56082	seeing that you were about five times as pretty as every other woman in
56155	the room. No thanks to his gallantry for that. Well, he certainly is
56225	very agreeable, and I give you leave to like him. You have liked many a
56298	stupider person.”
56319	
56321	“Dear Lizzy!”
56340

56417	You never see a fault in anybody. All the world are good and agreeable

56564

57144	
57146	“Certainly not, at first; but they are very pleasing women when you
57217	converse with them. Miss Bingley is to live with her brother, and keep
57289	his house; and I am much mistaken if we shall not find a very charming
57361	neighbour in her.”
57383	
57385	Elizabeth listened in silence, but was not convinced: their behaviour at
57459	the assembly had not been calculated to please in general; and with more
57533	quickness of observation and less pliancy of temper than her sister, and
57607	with a judgment, too, unassailed by any attention to herself, she was
57678	very little disposed to approve them. They were, in fact, very fine
57747	ladies; not deficient in good-humour when they were pleased, nor in the
57820	power of being agreeable where they chose it; but proud and conceited.
57892	They were rather handsome; had been educated in one of the first private
57966	seminaries in town; had a fortune of twenty thousand pounds; were in the
58040	habit of spending more than they ought, and of associating with people
58112	of rank; and were, therefore, in every respect entitled to think well of
58186	themselves and meanly of others. They were of a respectable family in
58257	the north of England; a circumstance more deeply impressed on their
58326	memories than that their brother’s fortune and their own had been
58395	acquired by trade.
58415	
58417	Mr. Bingley inherited property to the amount of nearly a hundred
58483	thousand pounds from his father, who had intended to purchase an estate,
58557	but did not live to do it. Mr. Bingley intended it likewise, and
58623	sometimes made choice of his county; but, as he was now provided with a
58696	good house and the liberty of a manor, it was doubtful to many of those
58769	who best knew the easiness of his temper, whether he might not spend the
58843	remainder of his days at Netherfield, and leave the next generation to
58915	purchase.
58926	
58928	His sisters were very anxious for his having an estate of his own; but
59000	though he was now established only as a tenant, Miss Bingley was by no
59072	means unwilling to preside at his table; nor was Mrs. Hurst, who had
59142	married a man of more fashion than fortune, less disposed to consider
59213	his house as her home when it suited her. Mr. Bingley had not been of
59284	age two years when he was tempted, by an accidental recommendation, to
59356	look at Netherfield House. He did look at it, and into it, for half an
59428	hour; was pleased with the situation and the principal rooms, satisfied
59501	with what the owner said in its praise, and took it immediately.
59567	
59569	Between him and Darcy there was a very steady friendship, in spite of a
59642	great opposition of character. Bingley was endeared to Darcy by the
59711	easiness, openness, and ductility of his temper, though no disposition
59783	could offer a greater contrast to his own, and though with his own he
59854	never appeared dissatisfied. On the strength of Darcy’s regard, Bingley
59929	had the firmest reliance, and of his judgment the highest opinion. In
60000	understanding, Darcy was the superior. Bingley was by no means
60064	deficient; but Darcy was clever. He was at the same time haughty,
60131	reserved, and fastidious; and his manners, though well bred, were not
60202	inviting. In that respect his friend had greatly the advantage. Bingley
60275	was sure of being liked wherever he appeared; Darcy was continually
60344	giving offence.
60361	
60363	The manner in which they spoke of the Meryton assembly was sufficiently
60436	characteristic. Bingley had never met with pleasanter people or prettier
60510	girls in his life; everybody had been most kind and attentive to him;
60581	there had been no formality, no stiffness; he had soon felt acquainted
60653	with all the room; and as to Miss Bennet, he could not conceive an angel
60727	more beautiful. Darcy, on the contrary, had seen a collection of people
60800	in whom there was little beauty and no fashion, for none of whom he had
60873	felt the smallest interest, and from none received either attention or
60945	pleasure. Miss Bennet he acknowledged to be pretty; but she smiled too
61017	much.
61024	
61026	Mrs. Hurst and her sister allowed it to be so; but still they admired
61097	her and liked her, and pronounced her to be a sweet girl, and one whom
61169	they should not object to know more of. Miss Bennet was therefore
61236	established as a sweet girl; and their brother felt authorized by such
61308	commendation to think of her as he chose.

61420	CHAPTER V.
61432	
61434	
61436	[Illustration]
61452	
61454	Within a short walk of Longbourn lived a family with whom the Bennets
61525	were particularly intimate. Sir William Lucas had been formerly in trade
61599	in Meryton, where he had made a tolerable fortune, and risen to the
61668	honour of knighthood by an address to the king during his mayoralty. The
61742	distinction had, perhaps, been felt too strongly. It had given him a
61812	disgust to his business and to his residence in a small market town;
61882	and, quitting them both, he had removed with his family to a house about
61956	a mile from Meryton, denominated from that period Lucas Lodge; where he
62029	could think with pleasure of his own importance, and, unshackled by
62098	business, occupy himself solely in being civil to all the world. For,
62169	though elated by his rank, it did not render him supercilious; on the
62240	contrary, he was all attention to everybody. By nature inoffensive,
62309	friendly, and obliging, his presentation at St. James’s had made him
62381	courteous.
62393	
62395	Lady Lucas was a very good kind of woman, not too clever to be a
62461	valuable neighbour to Mrs. Bennet. They had several children. The eldest
62535	of them, a sensible, intelligent young woman, about twenty-seven, was
62606	Elizabeth’s intimate friend.
62638	
62640	That the Miss Lucases and the Miss Bennets should meet to talk over a
62711	ball was absolutely necessary; and the morning after the assembly
62778	brought the former to Longbourn to hear and to communicate.
62839	
62841	“_You_ began the evening well, Charlotte,” said Mrs. Bennet, with civil
62918	self-command, to Miss Lucas. “_You_ were Mr. Bingley’s first choice.”
62995	
62997	“Yes; but he seemed to like his second better.”
63050	
63052	“Oh, you mean Jane, I suppose, because he danced with her twice. To be
63126	sure that _did_ seem as if he admired her--indeed, I rather believe he
63198	_did_--I heard something about it--but I hardly know what--something
63268	about Mr. Robinson.”
63292	
63294	“Perhaps you mean what I overheard between him and Mr. Robinson: did not
63370	I mention it to you? Mr. Robinson’s asking him how he liked our Meryton
63445	assemblies, and whether he did not think there were a great many pretty
63518	women in the room, and _which_ he thought the prettiest? and his
63584	answering immediately to the last question, ‘Oh, the eldest Miss Bennet,
63660	beyond a doubt: there cannot be two opinions on that point.’”
63727	
63729	“Upon my word! Well, that was very decided, indeed--that does seem as
63802	if--but, however, it may all come to nothing, you know.”
63862	
63864	“_My_ overhearings were more to the purpose than _yours_, Eliza,” said
63940	Charlotte. “Mr. Darcy is not so well worth listening to as his friend,
64014	is he? Poor Eliza! to be only just _tolerable_.”
64066	
64068	“I beg you will not put it into Lizzy’s head to be vexed by his
64137	ill-treatment, for he is such a disagreeable man that it would be quite
64210	a misfortune to be liked by him. Mrs. Long told me last night that he
64281	sat close to her for half an hour without once opening his lips.”
64350	
64352	[Illustration: “Without once opening his lips”
64404	
64406	[_Copyright 1894 by George Allen._]]
64444	
64446	“Are you quite sure, ma’am? Is not there a little mistake?” said Jane.
64524	“I certainly saw Mr. Darcy speaking to her.”
64574	
64576	“Ay, because she asked him at last how he liked Netherfield, and he
64647	could not help answering her; but she said he seemed very angry at being
64721	spoke to.”
64735	
64737	“Miss Bingley told me,” said Jane, “that he never speaks much unless
64813	among his intimate acquaintance. With _them_ he is remarkably
64876	agreeable.”
64891	
64893	“I do not believe a word of it, my dear. If he had been so very
64960	agreeable, he would have talked to Mrs. Long. But I can guess how it
65030	was; everybody says that he is eat up with pride, and I dare say he had
65103	heard somehow that Mrs. Long does not keep a carriage, and had to come
65175	to the ball in a hack chaise.”
65209	
65211	“I do not mind his not talking to Mrs. Long,” said Miss Lucas, “but I
65288	wish he had danced with Eliza.”
65323	
65325	“Another time, Lizzy,” said her mother, “I would not dance with _him_,
65403	if I were you.”
65422	
65424	“I believe, ma’am, I may safely promise you _never_ to dance with him.”
65503	
65505	“His pride,” said Miss Lucas, “does not offend _me_ so much as pride
65581	often does, because there is an excuse for it. One cannot wonder that so
65655	very fine a young man, with family, fortune, everything in his favour,
65727	should think highly of himself. If I may so express it, he has a _right_
65801	to be proud.”
65818	
65820	“That is very true,” replied Elizabeth, “and I could easily forgive
65895	_his_ pride, if he had not mortified _mine_.”
65944	
65946	“Pride,” observed Mary, who piqued herself upon the solidity of her
66019	reflections, “is a very common failing, I believe. By all that I have
66092	ever read, I am convinced that it is very common indeed; that human
66161	nature is particularly prone to it, and that there are very few of us
66232	who do not cherish a feeling of self-complacency on the score of some
66303	quality or other, real or imaginary. Vanity and pride are different
66372	things, though the words are often used synonymously. A person may be
66443	proud without being vain. Pride relates more to our opinion of
66507	ourselves; vanity to what we would have others think of us.”
66571	
66573	“If I were as rich as Mr. Darcy,” cried a young Lucas, who came with his
66651	sisters, “I should not care how proud I was. I would keep a pack of
66722	foxhounds, and drink a bottle of wine every day.”
66775	
66777	“Then you would drink a great deal more than you ought,” said Mrs.
66849	Bennet; “and if I were to see you at it, I should take away your bottle
66924	directly.”
66938	
66940	The boy protested that she should not; she continued to declare that she
67014	would; and the argument ended only with the visit.

67116	CHAPTER VI.
67129	
67131	
67133	[Illustration]
67149	
67151	The ladies of Longbourn soon waited on those of Netherfield. The visit
67223	was returned in due form. Miss Bennet’s pleasing manners grew on the
67295	good-will of Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley; and though the mother was
67364	found to be intolerable, and the younger sisters not worth speaking to,
67437	a wish of being better acquainted with _them_ was expressed towards the
67510	two eldest. By Jane this attention was received with the greatest
67577	pleasure; but Elizabeth still saw superciliousness in their treatment of
67651	everybody, hardly excepting even her sister, and could not like them;
67722	though their kindness to Jane, such as it was, had a value, as arising,
67795	in all probability, from the influence of their brother’s admiration. It
67871	was generally evident, whenever they met, that he _did_ admire her; and
67944	to _her_ it was equally evident that Jane was yielding to the preference
68018	which she had begun to entertain for him from the first, and was in a
68089	way to be very much in love; but she considered with pleasure that it
68160	was not likely to be discovered by the world in general, since Jane
68229	united with great strength of feeling, a composure of temper and an
68298	uniform cheerfulness of manner, which would guard her from the
68362	suspicions of the impertinent. She mentioned this to her friend, Miss
68433	Lucas.
68441	
68443	“It may, perhaps, be pleasant,” replied Charlotte, “to be able to impose
68523	on the public in such a case; but it is sometimes a disadvantage to be
68595	so very guarded. If a woman conceals her affection with the same skill
68667	from the object of it, she may lose the opportunity of fixing him; and
68739	it will then be but poor consolation to believe the world equally in the
68813	dark. There is so much of gratitude or vanity in almost every
68876	attachment, that it is not safe to leave any to itself. We can all
68944	_begin_ freely--a slight preference is natural enough; but there are
69014	very few of us who have heart enough to be really in love without
69081	encouragement. In nine cases out of ten, a woman had better show _more_
69154	affection than she feels. Bingley likes your sister undoubtedly; but he
69227	may never do more than like her, if she does not help him on.”
69293	
69295	“But she does help him on, as much as her nature will allow. If _I_ can
69370	perceive her regard for him, he must be a simpleton indeed not to
69437	discover it too.”
69458	
69460	“Remember, Eliza, that he does not know Jane’s disposition as you do.”
69538	
69540	“But if a woman is partial to a man, and does not endeavor to conceal
69613	it, he must find it out.”
69642	
69644	“Perhaps he must, if he sees enough of her. But though Bingley and Jane
69719	meet tolerably often, it is never for many hours together; and as they
69791	always see each other in large mixed parties, it is impossible that
69860	every moment should be employed in conversing together. Jane should
69929	therefore make the most of every half hour in which she can command his
70002	attention. When she is secure of him, there will be leisure for falling
70075	in love as much as she chooses.”
70111	
70113	“Your plan is a good one,” replied Elizabeth, “where nothing is in
70187	question but the desire of being well married; and if I were determined
70260	to get a rich husband, or any husband, I dare say I should adopt it. But
70334	these are not Jane’s feelings; she is not acting by design. As yet she
70408	cannot even be certain of the degree of her own regard, nor of its
70476	reasonableness. She has known him only a fortnight. She danced four
70545	dances with him at Meryton; she saw him one morning at his own house,
70616	and has since dined in company with him four times. This is not quite
70687	enough to make her understand his character.”
70736	
70738	“Not as you represent it. Had she merely _dined_ with him, she might
70810	only have discovered whether he had a good appetite; but you must
70877	remember that four evenings have been also spent together--and four
70946	evenings may do a great deal.”
70980	
70982	“Yes: these four evenings have enabled them to ascertain that they both
71057	like Vingt-un better than Commerce, but with respect to any other
71124	leading characteristic, I do not imagine that much has been unfolded.”
71198	
71200	“Well,” said Charlotte, “I wish Jane success with all my heart; and if
71278	she were married to him to-morrow, I should think she had as good a
71347	chance of happiness as if she were to be studying his character for a
71418	twelvemonth. Happiness in marriage is entirely a matter of chance. If
71489	the dispositions of the parties are ever so well known to each other, or
71563	ever so similar beforehand, it does not advance their felicity in the
71634	least. They always continue to grow sufficiently unlike afterwards to
71705	have their share of vexation; and it is better to know as little as
71774	possible of the defects of the person with whom you are to pass your
71844	life.”
71854	
71856	“You make me laugh, Charlotte; but it is not sound. You know it is not
71930	sound, and that you would never act in this way yourself.”
71992	
71994	Occupied in observing Mr. Bingley’s attention to her sister, Elizabeth
72068	was far from suspecting that she was herself becoming an object of some
72141	interest in the eyes of his friend. Mr. Darcy had at first scarcely
72210	allowed her to be pretty: he had looked at her without admiration at the
72284	ball; and when they next met, he looked at her only to criticise. But no
72358	sooner had he made it clear to himself and his friends that she had
72427	hardly a good feature in her face, than he began to find it was rendered
72501	uncommonly intelligent by the beautiful expression of her dark eyes. To
72574	this discovery succeeded some others equally mortifying. Though he had
72646	detected with a critical eye more than one failure of perfect symmetry
72718	in her form, he was forced to acknowledge her figure to be light and
72788	pleasing; and in spite of his asserting that her manners were not those
72861	of the fashionable world, he was caught by their easy playfulness. Of
72932	this she was perfectly unaware: to her he was only the man who made
73001	himself agreeable nowhere, and who had not thought her handsome enough
73073	to dance with.
73089	
73091	He began to wish to know more of her; and, as a step towards conversing
73164	with her himself, attended to her conversation with others. His doing so
73238	drew her notice. It was at Sir William Lucas’s, where a large party were
73314	assembled.
73326	
73328	“What does Mr. Darcy mean,” said she to Charlotte, “by listening to my
73406	conversation with Colonel Forster?”
73445	
73447	“That is a question which Mr. Darcy only can answer.”
73506	
73508	“But if he does it any more, I shall certainly let him know that I see
73582	what he is about. He has a very satirical eye, and if I do not begin by
73655	being impertinent myself, I shall soon grow afraid of him.”
73718	
73720	[Illustration: “The entreaties of several” [_Copyright 1894 by George
73795	Allen._]]
73806	
73808	On his approaching them soon afterwards, though without seeming to have
73881	any intention of speaking, Miss Lucas defied her friend to mention such
73954	a subject to him, which immediately provoking Elizabeth to do it, she
74025	turned to him and said,--
74052	
74054	“Did not you think, Mr. Darcy, that I expressed myself uncommonly well
74128	just now, when I was teasing Colonel Forster to give us a ball at
74195	Meryton?”
74208	
74210	“With great energy; but it is a subject which always makes a lady
74279	energetic.”
74294	
74296	“You are severe on us.”
74325	
74327	“It will be _her_ turn soon to be teased,” said Miss Lucas. “I am going
74406	to open the instrument, Eliza, and you know what follows.”
74468	
74470	“You are a very strange creature by way of a friend!--always wanting me
74545	to play and sing before anybody and everybody! If my vanity had taken a
74618	musical turn, you would have been invaluable; but as it is, I would
74687	really rather not sit down before those who must be in the habit of
74756	hearing the very best performers.” On Miss Lucas’s persevering, however,
74834	she added, “Very well; if it must be so, it must.” And gravely glancing
74911	at Mr. Darcy, “There is a very fine old saying, which everybody here is
74986	of course familiar with--‘Keep your breath to cool your porridge,’--and
75063	I shall keep mine to swell my song.”
75103	
75105	Her performance was pleasing, though by no means capital. After a song
75177	or two, and before she could reply to the entreaties of several that she
75251	would sing again, she was eagerly succeeded at the instrument by her
75321	sister Mary, who having, in consequence of being the only plain one in
75393	the family, worked hard for knowledge and accomplishments, was always
75464	impatient for display.
75488	
75490	Mary had neither genius nor taste; and though vanity had given her
75558	application, it had given her likewise a pedantic air and conceited
75627	manner, which would have injured a higher degree of excellence than she
75700	had reached. Elizabeth, easy and unaffected, had been listened to with
75772	much more pleasure, though not playing half so well; and Mary, at the
75843	end of a long concerto, was glad to purchase praise and gratitude by
75913	Scotch and Irish airs, at the request of her younger sisters, who with
75985	some of the Lucases, and two or three officers, joined eagerly in
76052	dancing at one end of the room.
76085	
76087	Mr. Darcy stood near them in silent indignation at such a mode of
76154	passing the evening, to the exclusion of all conversation, and was too
76226	much engrossed by his own thoughts to perceive that Sir William Lucas
76297	was his neighbour, till Sir William thus began:--
76348	
76350	“What a charming amusement for young people this is, Mr. Darcy! There is
76426	nothing like dancing, after all. I consider it as one of the first
76494	refinements of polished societies.”
76533	
76535	“Certainly, sir; and it has the advantage also of being in vogue amongst
76611	the less polished societies of the world: every savage can dance.”
76681	
76683	Sir William only smiled. “Your friend performs delightfully,” he
76753	continued, after a pause, on seeing Bingley join the group; “and I doubt
76829	not that you are an adept in the science yourself, Mr. Darcy.”
76895	
76897	“You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir.”
76949	
76951	“Yes, indeed, and received no inconsiderable pleasure from the sight. Do
77027	you often dance at St. James’s?”
77065	
77067	“Never, sir.”
77086	
77088	“Do you not think it would be a proper compliment to the place?”
77158	
77160	“It is a compliment which I never pay to any place if I can avoid it.”
77236	
77238	“You have a house in town, I conclude?”
77283	
77285	Mr. Darcy bowed.
77303	
77305	“I had once some thoughts of fixing in town myself, for I am fond of
77377	superior society; but I did not feel quite certain that the air of
77445	London would agree with Lady Lucas.”
77485	
77487	He paused in hopes of an answer: but his companion was not disposed to
77559	make any; and Elizabeth at that instant moving towards them, he was
77628	struck with the notion of doing a very gallant thing, and called out to
77701	her,--
77709	
77711	“My dear Miss Eliza, why are not you dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must allow
77786	me to present this young lady to you as a very desirable partner. You
77857	cannot refuse to dance, I am sure, when so much beauty is before you.”
77931	And, taking her hand, he would have given it to Mr. Darcy, who, though
78003	extremely surprised, was not unwilling to receive it, when she instantly
78077	drew back, and said with some discomposure to Sir William,--
78139	
78141	“Indeed, sir, I have not the least intention of dancing. I entreat you
78215	not to suppose that I moved this way in order to beg for a partner.”
78287	
78289	Mr. Darcy, with grave propriety, requested to be allowed the honour of
78361	her hand, but in vain. Elizabeth was determined; nor did Sir William at
78434	all shake her purpose by his attempt at persuasion.
78487	
78489	“You excel so much in the dance, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deny me
78565	the happiness of seeing you; and though this gentleman dislikes the
78634	amusement in general, he can have no objection, I am sure, to oblige us
78707	for one half hour.”
78730	
78732	“Mr. Darcy is all politeness,” said Elizabeth, smiling.
78793	
78795	“He is, indeed: but considering the inducement, my dear Miss Eliza, we
78869	cannot wonder at his complaisance; for who would object to such a
78936	partner?”
78949	
78951	Elizabeth looked archly, and turned away. Her resistance had not injured
79025	her with the gentleman, and he was thinking of her with some
79087	complacency, when thus accosted by Miss Bingley,--
79139	
79141	“I can guess the subject of your reverie.”
79189	
79191	“I should imagine not.”
79220	
79222	“You are considering how insupportable it would be to pass many
79289	evenings in this manner,--in such society; and, indeed, I am quite of
79360	your opinion. I was never more annoyed! The insipidity, and yet the
79429	noise--the nothingness, and yet the self-importance, of all these
79496	people! What would I give to hear your strictures on them!”
79559	
79561	“Your conjecture is totally wrong, I assure you. My mind was more
79630	agreeably engaged. I have been meditating on the very great pleasure
79700	which a pair of fine eyes in the face of a pretty woman can bestow.”
79772	
79774	Miss Bingley immediately fixed her eyes on his face, and desired he
79843	would tell her what lady had the credit of inspiring such reflections.
79915	Mr. Darcy replied, with great intrepidity,--
79961	
79963	“Miss Elizabeth Bennet.”
79993	
79995	“Miss Elizabeth Bennet!” repeated Miss Bingley. “I am all astonishment.
80074	How long has she been such a favourite? and pray when am I to wish you
80146	joy?”
80155	
80157	“That is exactly the question which I expected you to ask. A lady’s
80230	imagination is very rapid; it jumps from admiration to love, from love
80302	to matrimony, in a moment. I knew you would be wishing me joy.”
80369	
80371	“Nay, if you are so serious about it, I shall consider the matter as
80443	absolutely settled. You will have a charming mother-in-law, indeed, and
80516	of course she will be always at Pemberley with you.”
80572	
80574	He listened to her with perfect indifference, while she chose to
80640	entertain herself in this manner; and as his composure convinced her
80710	that all was safe, her wit flowed along.

80861	CHAPTER VII.
80875	
80877	
80879	[Illustration]
80895	
80897	Mr. Bennet’s property consisted almost entirely in an estate of two
80968	thousand a year, which, unfortunately for his daughters, was entailed,
81040	in default of heirs male, on a distant relation; and their mother’s
81111	fortune, though ample for her situation in life, could but ill supply
81182	the deficiency of his. Her father had been an attorney in Meryton, and
81254	had left her four thousand pounds.
81290	
81292	She had a sister married to a Mr. Philips, who had been a clerk to their
81366	father and succeeded him in the business, and a brother settled in
81434	London in a respectable line of trade.
81474	
81476	The village of Longbourn was only one mile from Meryton; a most
81541	convenient distance for the young ladies, who were usually tempted
81609	thither three or four times a week, to pay their duty to their aunt, and
81683	to a milliner’s shop just over the way. The two youngest of the family,
81758	Catherine and Lydia, were particularly frequent in these attentions:
81828	their minds were more vacant than their sisters’, and when nothing
81898	better offered, a walk to Meryton was necessary to amuse their morning
81970	hours and furnish conversation for the evening; and, however bare of
82040	news the country in general might be, they always contrived to learn
82110	some from their aunt. At present, indeed, they were well supplied both

90074	assembled, and where her appearance created a great deal of surprise.

90214	dirty weather, and by herself, was almost incredible to Mrs. Hurst and

90889	Bennet had slept ill, and though up, was very feverish, and not well

91024	immediately; and Jane, who had only been withheld by the fear of giving
91097	alarm or inconvenience, from expressing in her note how much she longed
91170	for such a visit, was delighted at her entrance. She was not equal,

91449	her.

91530	began to like them herself, when she saw how much affection and
91595	solicitude they showed for Jane. The apothecary came; and having
91661	examined his patient, said, as might be supposed, that she had caught a
91734	violent cold, and that they must endeavour to get the better of it;

91877	was followed readily, for the feverish symptoms increased, and her head
91950	ached acutely. Elizabeth did not quit her room for a moment, nor were
92021	the other ladies often absent; the gentlemen being out, they had in fact

92796	At five o’clock the two ladies retired to dress, and at half-past six
92869	Elizabeth was summoned to dinner. To the civil inquiries which then
92938	poured in, and amongst which she had the pleasure of distinguishing the
93011	much superior solicitude of Mr. Bingley, she could not make a very
93079	favourable answer. Jane was by no means better. The sisters, on hearing
93152	this, repeated three or four times how much they were grieved, how
93220	shocking it was to have a bad cold, and how excessively they disliked
93291	being ill themselves; and then thought no more of the matter: and their
93364	indifference towards Jane, when not immediately before them, restored
93435	Elizabeth to the enjoyment of all her original dislike.
93492	
93494	Their brother, indeed, was the only one of the party whom she could
93563	regard with any complacency. His anxiety for Jane was evident, and his
93635	attentions to herself most pleasing; and they prevented her feeling
93704	herself so much an intruder as she believed she was considered by the
93775	others. She had very little notice from any but him. Miss Bingley was
93846	engrossed by Mr. Darcy, her sister scarcely less so; and as for Mr.
93915	Hurst, by whom Elizabeth sat, he was an indolent man, who lived only to
93988	eat, drink, and play at cards, who, when he found her prefer a plain
94058	dish to a ragout, had nothing to say to her.

94390	thought the same, and added,--

104441	CHAPTER IX.

104456	
104458	[Illustration]
104474	
104476	Elizabeth passed the chief of the night in her sister’s room, and in the
104552	morning had the pleasure of being able to send a tolerable answer to the
104626	inquiries which she very early received from Mr. Bingley by a housemaid,
104700	and some time afterwards from the two elegant ladies who waited on his
104772	sisters. In spite of this amendment, however, she requested to have a
104843	note sent to Longbourn, desiring her mother to visit Jane, and form her
104916	own judgment of her situation. The note was immediately despatched, and
104989	its contents as quickly complied with. Mrs. Bennet, accompanied by her
105061	two youngest girls, reached Netherfield soon after the family breakfast.
105135	
105137	Had she found Jane in any apparent danger, Mrs. Bennet would have been
105209	very miserable; but being satisfied on seeing her that her illness was
105281	not alarming, she had no wish of her recovering immediately, as her
105350	restoration to health would probably remove her from Netherfield. She
105421	would not listen, therefore, to her daughter’s proposal of being carried
105497	home; neither did the apothecary, who arrived about the same time, think
105571	it at all advisable. After sitting a little while with Jane, on Miss
105641	Bingley’s appearance and invitation, the mother and three daughters all
105716	attended her into the breakfast parlour. Bingley met them with hopes
105786	that Mrs. Bennet had not found Miss Bennet worse than she expected.
105855	
105857	“Indeed I have, sir,” was her answer. “She is a great deal too ill to be
105937	moved. Mr. Jones says we must not think of moving her. We must trespass
106010	a little longer on your kindness.”
106048	
106050	“Removed!” cried Bingley. “It must not be thought of. My sister, I am
106127	sure, will not hear of her removal.”

290086	side by preparations for the reception of his bride, as he had reason to
290160	hope, that shortly after his next return into Hertfordshire, the day
290230	would be fixed that was to make him the happiest of men. He took leave
290302	of his relations at Longbourn with as much solemnity as before; wished
290374	his fair cousins health and happiness again, and promised their father
290446	another letter of thanks.

290965	than Mrs. Bennet and Mrs. Philips, was an amiable, intelligent, elegant
291038	woman, and a great favourite with her Longbourn nieces. Between the two
291111	eldest and herself especially, there subsisted a very particular regard.

291599	girls had been on the point of marriage, and after all there was nothing
291673	in it.

312587	Elizabeth to Hunsford. She had not at first thought very seriously of
312658	going thither; but Charlotte, she soon found, was depending on the

312795	pleasure as well as greater certainty. Absence had increased her desire
312868	of seeing Charlotte again, and weakened her disgust of Mr. Collins.

319921	Every object in the next day’s journey was new and interesting to
319990	Elizabeth; and her spirits were in a state of enjoyment; for she had
320060	seen her sister looking so well as to banish all fear for her health,
320131	and the prospect of her northern tour was a constant source of delight.

320279	search of the Parsonage, and every turning expected to bring it in view.
320353	The paling of Rosings park was their boundary on one side. Elizabeth
320423	smiled at the recollection of all that she had heard of its inhabitants.

320567	road, the house standing in it, the green pales and the laurel hedge,
320638	everything declared they were arriving. Mr. Collins and Charlotte
320705	appeared at the door, and the carriage stopped at the small gate, which
320778	led by a short gravel walk to the house, amidst the nods and smiles of
320850	the whole party. In a moment they were all out of the chaise, rejoicing
